final-exam-#1-004.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. Start with 3 VA per square foot of living space (outside dimensions, minus open porches and unfinished spaces), add 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, then shrink the subtotal with the demand factor (first 3,000 VA at full value, 3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, the remainder at 25%). Ranges and dryers use their own tables — a range nameplate is only the starting point. Heat and AC: count the larger one, never both.

This is a load-calculation question. Numbers in the question: 5,000 sq. ft. Find the unit load for the occupancy, multiply by the area or quantity, and apply any demand factor the question allows.

Electrical Theory • Power Equation (Watt's Law)
In the electrical power equation W = E x I (Watts = Volts x Amperes), the letter I traditionally designates 'Intensity of current' (from the French 'intensité du courant'), representing current flow in amperes.

I stands for intensity of current, the current flow measured in amperes. Not A: Intrinsic circuit is not an electrical variable; I in the power formula is current in amperes. Not B: Electromotive force is the E (volts) in W = E x I, not the I. Not D: Isotopic character is a chemistry idea, unrelated to the current variable I.

final-exam-#1-019.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one (two 2,000-ohm resistors = 1,000 ohms). Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s, so 90° takes a quarter of that — 1/240 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

In plain terms, the question is: "What does the alpha character I represent when stating the equation W = E x I?" Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

A stop pushbutton switch has normally closed (NC) contacts that must open the control circuit to de-energize the magnetic holding coil. Therefore, the stop switch is always wired in series with the motor control circuit.

Not C: Series-parallel is wrong; multiple stop buttons all go in series, while start buttons go in parallel. Not D: Parallel is how start buttons connect; a stop button in parallel could not break the control circuit.

final-exam-#3-045.prompt: The total number of AC cycles completed in one second is the current's ___.
final-exam-#3-045.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one (two 2,000-ohm resistors = 1,000 ohms). Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s, so 90° takes a quarter of that — 1/240 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

Hazardous locations are sorted by what's in the air. Class I means flammable gases or vapors (gasoline, spray booths). Class II means combustible dust (grain, flour, coal). final-exam-#5-066.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one (two 2,000-ohm resistors = 1,000 ohms). Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s, so 90° takes a quarter of that — 1/240 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

Where the heaters are rated 50 kW or more, the conductors supplying the supplementary overcurrent protective devices specified in 425.22(C) shall be permitted to be sized at not less than 100 percent of the nameplate rating of the heater, provided all of the following conditions are met:

final-exam-#3-003.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

In plain terms, the question is: "The conductors supplying the supplementary overcurrent protective devices for fixed industrial process heating equipment shall be…" Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

final-exam-#3-070.prompt: The symbol for a three-phase delta wound generator consists of a circle with a ___ scribed inside.
final-exam-#3-070.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one (two 2,000-ohm resistors = 1,000 ohms). Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s, so 90° takes a quarter of that — 1/240 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

In plain terms, the question is: "The symbol for a three-phase delta wound generator consists of a circle with a ___ scribed inside." Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement

open-book-exam-#1-021.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. Start with 3 VA per square foot of living space (outside dimensions, minus open porches and unfinished spaces), add 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, then shrink the subtotal with the demand factor (first 3,000 VA at full value, 3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, the remainder at 25%). Ranges and dryers use their own tables — a range nameplate is only the starting point. Heat and AC: count the larger one, never both.

This is a load-calculation question. Numbers in the question: 5,000 sq. ft. Find the unit load for the occupancy, multiply by the area or quantity, and apply any demand factor the question allows.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS

Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. 310.14(A)(3) Temperature Limitation of Conductors
No conductor shall be used in such a manner that its operating temperature exceeds that designated for the type of insulated conductor involved. In no case shall conductors be associated together in such a way, with respect to type of circuit, the wiring method employed, or the number of conductors, that the limiting temperature of any conductor is exceeded.
Informational Note No. 1: See Table 310.4(1) and Table 315.10(A) for the temperature rating of a conductor that is the maximum temperature, at any location along its length, that the conductor can withstand over a prolonged time period without serious degradation. The ampacity tables of Article 310 and the ampacity tables of Informative Annex B, the ambient temperature correction factors in 310.15(B), and the notes to the tables provide guidance for coordinating conductor sizes, types, ampacities, ambient temperatures, and number of associated conductors. The principal determinants of operating temperature are as follows:
(1) Ambient temperature - ambient temperature may vary along the conductor length as well as from time to time.
(2) Heat generated internally in the conductor as the result of load current flow, including fundamental and harmonic currents.
(3) The rate at which generated heat dissipates into the ambient medium. Thermal insulation that covers or surrounds conductors affects the rate of heat dissipation.
(4) Adjacent load-carrying conductors - adjacent conductors have the dual effect of raising the ambient temperature and impeding heat dissipation.
Informational Note No. 2: Refer to 110.14(C) for the temperature limitation of terminations.

Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. open-book-exam-#7-001.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

In plain terms, the question is: "Premises wiring shall not be ___ connected to a supply system unless the latter contains, for any grounded conductor of the interior system,…" Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

final-exam-#3-039.prompt: Central heating equipment, other than fixed electric space-heating equipment, must be supplied by a/an ___ branch circuit.
final-exam-#3-039.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Branch circuits are rated by their breaker: the standard sizes are 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amps. A multiwire (shared-neutral) circuit must open all its ungrounded legs together so no leg can stay live alone. And the number of circuits in a building comes from the total load divided by circuit size — fractional results always round up, because half a circuit doesn't exist.

In plain terms, the question is: "Central heating equipment, other than fixed electric space-heating equipment, must be supplied by a/an ___ branch circuit." Subject: branch circuit. Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS

An open resistor has a break in its resistive path, so the small test current from the ohmmeter's battery cannot flow through it. In a parallel circuit every branch is connected directly across the same two points of the source, so the voltage across each branch equals the source voltage. The branch currents divide according to each branch's resistance and add up to the total current.

Electrical Theory • Series Circuits and Lamp Resistance
A lamp's resistance is R = E² ÷ P, so a 25-watt lamp has more resistance than a 60-watt lamp (at 120 volts about 576 ohms versus 240 ohms). In a series circuit the same current flows through every part and is set by the total resistance. Swapping in the higher-resistance 25-watt lamp raises the total resistance and lowers the current, so the heater's output (I² × R) decreases.

Every branch of a parallel circuit is connected across the same source, so the voltage across each branch is equal no matter what its resistance is. With unequal resistances the branch currents (I = E ÷ R) and the branch powers (P = E × I) are different.

final-exam-#2-017.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Phase Angle (ELI the ICE Man)
In an inductive circuit the voltage (E) leads the current (I): ELI. In a capacitive circuit the current (I) leads the voltage (E): ICE. A lagging current therefore means the circuit is inductive. At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel and the current is in phase with the voltage.

final-exam-#2-018.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Effective (RMS) Value
The effective, or root-mean-square (RMS), value of a sine wave is the value that produces the same heating as the same amount of direct current. It equals 0.707 times the peak value. Meters, nameplates, and the NEC use effective values: 120 volts ac means 120 volts RMS.

final-exam-#2-018.tip_short: The effective (RMS) value is 0.707 times the peak and gives the same heating as DC, so it is the value on meters and nameplates. Correct: C — effective.

final-exam-#2-019.gist: Wire resistance depends on how long the conductor is and how big it is. The question changes both at once and asks for the new resistance.
final-exam-#2-019.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Conductor Resistance
Resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area (R = K × L ÷ A). Tripling the length multiplies the resistance by 3, and halving the area multiplies it by 2.
choice_notes: 7.5 ohms matches no correct step; tripling the length and halving the area multiplies 5 ohms by 6.

Resistance is proportional to length and inverse to area: 5 ohms times 3 times 2 equals 30 ohms. Not A: 7.5 ohms matches no correct step; tripling the length and halving the area multiplies 5 ohms by 6. Not B: 15 ohms accounts only for the tripled length; halving the area doubles the resistance again. Not D: 50 ohms overshoots; the combined factor is 3 times 2, or 6, so 5 ohms becomes 30 ohms.
final-exam-#2-019.formula: R = K × L ÷ A: resistance rises in proportion to length and in inverse proportion to cross-sectional area. Apply both changes to the original 5 ohms.
final-exam-#2-019.worked: 5 Ω × 3 (three times the length) = 15 Ω; 15 Ω ÷ 0.5 (half the area) = 30 Ω.
final-exam-#2-019.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with General calculation, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

final-exam-#2-031.gist: Transformers pass energy from one winding to another without the windings ever touching. The question asks the name of that effect.
final-exam-#2-031.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Electromagnetic Induction
A changing current in one conductor sets up a changing magnetic field, and that field induces a voltage in a nearby conductor with no physical connection between them. This is how transformers, motors, and generators work.
choice_notes: Flux cutting describes how a conductor moving through a field gets a voltage; the overall process is called induction.
A short circuit is an unintended low-resistance path, not a way of producing voltage in another conductor.
Induction is the process by which a changing magnetic field from one conductor induces a voltage in another conductor.
Eddy currents are unwanted circulating currents induced in cores and metal parts, a side effect of induction.
final-exam-#2-031.tip_short: Induction: a changing magnetic field around one conductor induces a voltage in another with no mechanical connection. Correct: C — Induction. Not A: Flux cutting describes how a conductor moving through a field gets a voltage; the overall process is called induction.

final-exam-#2-032.gist: Current describes how much charge moves through a conductor. The question asks what that measurement counts.
final-exam-#2-032.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Current
Current is the rate of flow of electric charge past a point. One ampere is one coulomb of charge (about 6.24 x 10^18 electrons) passing a point each second.
choice_notes: Electron pressure is an old name for voltage (electromotive force), not current.
Current is the rate of charge flow, the number of electrons passing a point per second; one coulomb per second is one ampere.
Watts measure power, the product of voltage and current, not current itself.
Resistance, measured in ohms, is the opposition to current, not the current.
final-exam-#2-032.tip_short: Amperes count charge flow: one coulomb of electrons passing a point per second is one ampere. Correct: B — electrons passing a point per second.

final-exam-#2-033.gist: Resistance is a property of the conductors and connections, not of the voltage applied. The question asks which choice can actually change it.
final-exam-#2-033.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Resistance
The resistance of a conductor depends on its material, length, cross-sectional area, and temperature. A loose or corroded connection adds contact resistance to the circuit, which causes heating at the connection.
choice_notes: A loose or corroded connection adds contact resistance to the circuit, and that resistance heats the connection.
Changing the voltage changes the current (Ohm's law), not the resistance of the circuit.
A change in current follows from voltage or resistance; it does not itself change the resistance.
Induction creates a voltage; it does not change the resistance of the conductors.
final-exam-#2-033.tip_short: A loose connection adds resistance and heat; changing the voltage or current does not change a conductor's resistance (Ohm's law). Correct: A — a loose connection. A loose or corroded connection adds contact resistance to the circuit, and that resistance heats the connection. Not B: Changing the voltage changes the current (Ohm's law), not the resistance of the circuit.

final-exam-#2-034.gist: An AC sine wave rises in one direction, falls back, and then does the same in the other direction. The question asks how much of that wave one alternation covers.
final-exam-#2-034.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Alternating Current
One cycle of alternating current is made up of two alternations: one positive half and one negative half. An alternation is therefore one-half cycle; at 60 hertz there are 120 alternations per second.
choice_notes: An alternation is one-half cycle, the positive or the negative half of the sine wave.
One hertz is one full cycle per second, which contains two alternations.
An alternator is a machine that generates AC, not a part of the waveform.
Two cycles contain four alternations, not one.
final-exam-#2-034.tip_short: One cycle is two alternations, so an alternation is one-half cycle (120 per second at 60 Hz). Correct: A — one-half cycle. Not C: An alternator is a machine that generates AC, not a part of the waveform.

final-exam-#2-035.gist: A delicate meter movement cannot carry a large flow of charge, so a known low resistance carries most of it instead. The question asks what that arrangement lets the meter read.
final-exam-#2-035.reference_text:
Test Instruments • Ammeter Shunts
A shunt is a precise low-resistance element placed in series with the load and in parallel with a meter movement. The small voltage drop across it is proportional to the current, so the meter reads amperes.
choice_notes: Resistance is measured with an ohmmeter, which uses its own source, not a shunt.
Capacitance is measured with a capacitance meter or bridge, not a shunt.
A shunt carries most of the circuit current so the meter can read current from the small voltage drop across it.
Wattage is measured with a wattmeter that combines voltage and current; a shunt alone measures current.
final-exam-#2-035.tip_short: An ammeter shunt carries most of the current; the small voltage across it tells the meter the current. Correct: C — current.

final-exam-#2-036.gist: Paralleling conductors gives current a second path of the same size. The question asks what that does to the total resistance.
final-exam-#2-036.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Parallel Resistance
For equal resistances in parallel, the total resistance equals the resistance of one divided by the number of paths. Two equal conductors in parallel give one-half the resistance of one conductor.
choice_notes: One conductor's resistance is the value with a single path; adding a second equal path lowers it.
Twice the resistance is the series total of two equal conductors, not the parallel total.
Two equal resistances in parallel equal one-half the resistance of one conductor (R ÷ number of paths).
The resistance of both conductors in series would be twice one; in parallel the total is half of one.
final-exam-#2-036.tip_short: Equal resistances in parallel: divide one resistance by the number of paths, so two equal paths give half. Correct: C — one-half the resistance of one conductor. Not A: One conductor's resistance is the value with a single path; adding a second equal path lowers it. Not B: Twice the resistance is the series total of two equal conductors, not the parallel total.

final-exam-#2-037.gist: Motor branch circuits get their fuse or breaker size from a table of percentages of motor full-load current. The question asks the number of that table.

A protective device that has a rating or setting not exceeding the value calculated according to the values given in Table 430.52(C)(1) shall be used unless otherwise permitted in 430.52(C)(1)(a) or (C)(1)(b).

final-exam-#2-037.tip_short: Motor short-circuit and ground-fault protection is sized with Table 430.52(C)(1) percentages of the motor full-load current. Correct: B — 430.52(C)(1).

final-exam-#2-038.gist: A branch circuit takes its rating from the protective device, not from the wire. Adjustable breakers make a second word necessary. The question asks that word.

Marking is not the word in 210.18; the circuit is rated by the device's rating or setting.
210.18 rates branch circuits by the maximum permitted ampere rating or setting of the overcurrent device.
Rating is already in the stem; 210.18 says rating or setting of the overcurrent device.
final-exam-#2-038.tip_short: A branch circuit is rated by the ampere rating or setting of its overcurrent device, not by its conductor size. Correct: C — setting.

final-exam-#2-041.gist: The Article 100 definition of a luminaire lists what makes up a complete lighting unit and ends by excluding one item on its own. The question asks which choice the definition sets apart.
final-exam-#2-041.reference_text:
Article 100 Definitions — Luminaire
Luminaire. A complete lighting unit consisting of a light source such as a lamp or lamps, together with the parts designed to position the light source and connect it to the power supply. final-exam-#2-042.prompt: Galvanized steel, stainless steel, and ___ RMC shall be permitted under all atmospheric conditions and occupancies.

final-exam-#2-043.gist: Buried raceways corrode from aggressive backfill. The question asks what harmful backfill causes.
final-exam-#2-043.reference_text:
300.5(F) Backfill
Backfill that contains large rocks, paving materials, cinders, large or sharply angular substances, or corrosive material shall not be placed in an excavation where materials might damage raceways, cables, conductors, or other substructures or prevent adequate compaction of fill or contribute to corrosion of raceways, cables, or other substructures.
Where necessary to prevent physical damage to the raceway, cable, or conductor, protection shall be provided in the form of granular or selected material, suitable running boards, suitable sleeves, or other approved means.
choice_notes: Damage is already named earlier in 300.5(F); the final clause says corrosion.
Deterioration is not the word used; 300.5(F) says contribute to corrosion.
Aging is not mentioned in 300.5(F).
300.5(F) prohibits backfill that could contribute to corrosion of raceways, cables, or substructures.
final-exam-#2-043.tip_short: No rocks, cinders, or corrosive fill in trenches: they damage, prevent compaction, or cause corrosion. Correct: D — corrosion.

final-exam-#2-044.gist: A box carried only by its two conduit entries is exempt from separate support given compliant joints. The question asks how those conduits must connect.
final-exam-#2-044.reference_text:
314.23(E) Raceway-Supported Enclosure, Without Devices, Luminaires, or Lampholders
An enclosure that does not contain a device(s), other than splicing devices, or supports a luminaire(s), a lampholder, or other equipment and is supported by entering raceways shall not exceed 1650 cm3 (100 in.3) in size. It shall have threaded entries or identified hubs. It shall be supported by two or more conduits threaded wrenchtight into the enclosure or hubs. Each conduit shall be secured within 900 mm (3 ft) of the enclosure, or within 450 mm (18 in.) of the enclosure if all conduit entries are on the same side.
choice_notes: 314.23(E) requires two or more conduits threaded wrenchtight into the enclosure or identified hubs; simply being rigid nonmetallic conduit does not meet that requirement.
314.23(E) requires threaded entries or identified hubs, with conduits threaded wrenchtight into them.

Fitting shoulders with locknuts are not threaded entries; 314.23(E) requires threaded hubs or entries.
final-exam-#2-044.tip_short: A small box hung only on conduits needs two or more conduits threaded wrenchtight into the box or identified hubs. Correct: B — threaded into hubs identified for the purpose. 314.23(E) requires threaded entries or identified hubs, with conduits threaded wrenchtight into them. Not A: 314.23(E) requires two or more conduits threaded wrenchtight into the enclosure or identified hubs; simply being rigid nonmetallic conduit does not meet that requirement. Not C: Locknut connections are not threaded entries; 314.23(E) requires conduits threaded wrenchtight. Not D: Fitting shoulders with locknuts are not threaded entries; 314.23(E) requires threaded hubs or entries.

final-exam-#2-045.prompt: Conductors drawn from a copper-clad aluminum rod with the copper metallurgically bonded to an aluminum core. The copper forms a minimum of ___ percent of the cross-sectional area.
final-exam-#2-045.gist: Copper-clad aluminum conductors require a minimum copper percentage. The question asks the minimum percent copper.
final-exam-#2-045.reference_text:
310.3(B) Conductor Material
Conductors in this article shall be of copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum, unless otherwise specified. Aluminum and copper-clad aluminum shall comply with the following:
(3) For copper-clad aluminum conductors, the copper shall form a minimum 10 percent of the cross-sectional area of a solid conductor or each strand of a stranded conductor. The aluminum core of a copper-clad aluminum conductor shall be made of an AA-8000 series electrical grade aluminum alloy conductor material.
choice_notes: 310.3(B) says the copper shall form a minimum 10 percent of the cross-sectional area.
20 percent is not the Code value; 310.3(B) sets a 10 percent minimum.
40 percent is not the Code value; 310.3(B) sets a 10 percent minimum.
70 percent would make it mostly copper; 310.3(B) requires only 10 percent minimum.
final-exam-#2-045.tip_short: Copper-clad aluminum: a thin copper skin of at least 10 percent of the cross-sectional area. Correct: A — 10.

final-exam-#2-046.prompt: Concrete, brick, or tile walls are considered as being ___.
final-exam-#2-046.gist: With a concrete wall opposite the equipment, the required working depth changes. The question asks what concrete counts as.
final-exam-#2-046.reference_text:
110.26(A)(1) Depth of Working Space
Table 110.26(A)(1) Working Spaces
Nominal Voltage to Ground	Minimum Clear Distance
Condition 1	Condition 2	Condition 3
0—150	900 mm (3 ft)	900 mm (3 ft)	900 mm (3 ft)
151—600	900 mm (3 ft)	1.0 m (3 ft 6 in.)	1.2 m (4 ft)
601—1000	900 mm (3 ft)	1.2 m (4 ft)	1.5 m (5 ft)
Note: Where the conditions are as follows:
Condition 1 - Exposed live parts on one side of the working space and no live or grounded parts on the other side of the working space, or exposed live parts on both sides of the working space that are effectively guarded by insulating materials.
Condition 2 - Exposed live parts on one side of the working space and grounded parts on the other side of the working space. Concrete, brick, or tile walls shall be considered as grounded.
Condition 3 - Exposed live parts on both sides of the working space.

Masonry is not treated as an insulator for working space; the Code treats it as grounded.
Table 110.26(A)(1) Condition 2 says concrete, brick, or tile walls shall be considered as grounded.
Masonry walls can be damp and are not classified as dry locations in this rule.

final-exam-#2-046.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 110.26(A)(1) Condition 2, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

final-exam-#2-047.gist: An isolated-ground receptacle bears an identification mark on its face. The question asks what that mark is.
final-exam-#2-047.reference_text:
406.3(E) Isolated Ground Receptacles
Receptacles incorporating an isolated equipment grounding conductor connection intended for the reduction of electromagnetic interference as permitted in 250.146(D) shall be identified by an orange triangle located on the face of the receptacle.
(1) Isolated Equipment Grounding Conductor Required
Receptacles so identified shall be used only with equipment grounding conductors that are isolated in accordance with 250.146(D).
(2) Installation in Nonmetallic Boxes
Isolated ground receptacles installed in nonmetallic boxes shall be covered with a nonmetallic faceplate.
Exception: Where an isolated ground receptacle is installed in a nonmetallic box, a metal faceplate shall be permitted if the box contains a feature or accessory that permits the connection of the faceplate to the equipment grounding conductor.
choice_notes: CO/ALR marks a device rated for aluminum wire, not an isolated ground receptacle.
Faceplate thickness rules do not identify isolated ground receptacles; the orange triangle does.
A test button identifies a GFCI receptacle, not an isolated ground receptacle.
406.3(E) requires isolated ground receptacles to have an orange triangle on the face.
final-exam-#2-047.tip_short: Isolated ground receptacle equals orange triangle on the face, per 406.3(E). Correct: D — an orange triangle located on the face of the receptacle. 406.3(E) requires isolated ground receptacles to have an orange triangle on the face. Not A: CO/ALR marks a device rated for aluminum wire, not an isolated ground receptacle. Not B: Faceplate thickness rules do not identify isolated ground receptacles; the orange triangle does. Not C: A test button identifies a GFCI receptacle, not an isolated ground receptacle.

final-exam-#2-048.prompt: In a hospital Category 2 space, each patient bed location shall be provided with a minimum of ___ receptacles.
final-exam-#2-048.gist: A hospital bed location serves critical equipment requiring dedicated, reliable receptacles. The question asks the minimum outlets at each bed spot.
final-exam-#2-048.reference_text:
517.18(B)(1) Minimum Number and Supply
Each patient bed location shall be provided with a minimum of eight receptacles.
choice_notes: 3 single receptacles is far below the minimum of eight required by 517.18(B)(1).
2 single or 1 duplex is only two receptacles; 517.18(B)(1) requires eight.
2 duplex or 4 single is only four receptacles; 517.18(B)(1) requires eight.
517.18(B)(1) requires a minimum of eight receptacles, which is 4 duplex or 8 single.
final-exam-#2-048.tip_short: Category 2 (general care) patient bed locations need at least eight receptacles: four duplex devices provide eight. Correct: D — 4 duplex or 8 single.
final-exam-#2-048.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: receptacle outlet. Start with 517.18(B)(1), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

final-exam-#2-049.gist: A deck requires its own accessible receptacle within a maximum height. The question asks the maximum height above the deck floor.
final-exam-#2-049.reference_text:
210.52(E)(3) Balconies, Decks, and Porches
Balconies, decks, and porches that are within 102 mm (4 in.) horizontally of the dwelling unit shall have at least one receptacle outlet accessible from the balcony, deck, or porch. The receptacle outlet shall not be located more than 2.0 m (6 1/2 ft) above the balcony, deck, or porch walking surface.
choice_notes: 6 feet is lower than needed; 210.52(E)(3) allows up to 2.0 meters (6 1/2 feet).
210.52(E)(3) sets a maximum of 2.0 meters (6 1/2 feet), which is 6 feet 6 inches.
7 feet exceeds the 2.0 meter (6 1/2 feet) maximum in 210.52(E)(3).
8 feet exceeds the 2.0 meter (6 1/2 feet) maximum in 210.52(E)(3).
final-exam-#2-049.tip_short: Deck, balcony, and porch receptacle: no higher than 6 1/2 feet above the walking surface. Correct: B — 6'6". 210.52(E)(3) sets a maximum of 2.0 meters (6 1/2 feet), which is 6 feet 6 inches. Not A: 6 feet is lower than needed; 210.52(E)(3) allows up to 2.0 meters (6 1/2 feet). Not C: 7 feet exceeds the 2.0 meter (6 1/2 feet) maximum in 210.52(E)(3). Not D: 8 feet exceeds the 2.0 meter (6 1/2 feet) maximum in 210.52(E)(3).

final-exam-#2-050.gist: Two voltage levels in one raceway require cable with suitable separation construction. The question asks which insulation type the rule covers.
final-exam-#2-050.reference_text:
305.4 Conductors of Different Systems
Excitation, control, relay, and ammeter conductors used in connection with any individual motor or starter shall be permitted to occupy the same enclosure as the motor-circuit conductors.
Conductors of different voltage ratings shall be permitted in motors, transformers, switchgear, switchboards, control assemblies, and similar equipment.
If the conductors of each system in a manhole are permanently and effectively separated from the conductors of the other systems and securely fastened to racks, insulators, or other approved supports, conductors of different voltage ratings shall be permitted.
Conductors having nonshielded insulation and operating at different voltage levels shall not occupy the same enclosure, cable, or raceway.
choice_notes: Thermoset describes an insulation material type; 305.4 restricts nonshielded insulation.
Flame-retardant is a property, not the restriction; 305.4 addresses nonshielded insulation.
305.4 says conductors with nonshielded insulation at different voltage levels shall not share an enclosure.
Silicone rubber is an insulation material; 305.4 restricts nonshielded insulation.
final-exam-#2-050.tip_short: Over 1000 volts, nonshielded conductors at different voltages cannot share an enclosure, cable, or raceway. Correct: C — nonshielded.

final-exam-#2-051.gist: In AC circuits, coils and capacitors oppose current in addition to plain resistance. The question asks the name for the combined opposition.
final-exam-#2-051.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Impedance
Impedance (Z) is the total opposition to current in an AC circuit, combining resistance and the inductive and capacitive reactance. It is measured in ohms.
choice_notes: Impedance is the total opposition to current in an AC circuit, combining resistance and reactance, measured in ohms.
Conductance is the ease of current flow, the reciprocal of resistance, measured in siemens.
Reluctance is the opposition to magnetic flux in a magnetic circuit, not to current.
Resistance is only part of the AC opposition; it leaves out inductive and capacitive reactance.
final-exam-#2-051.tip_short: Impedance (Z, in ohms) is the total AC opposition: resistance plus inductive and capacitive reactance combined. Correct: A — impedance.

final-exam-#2-052.gist: A heater element is a fixed resistance, and its power depends on the square of the applied voltage. The question asks what happens to the heat at half the rated voltage.
final-exam-#2-052.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Power and Voltage
A resistive heater's power is P = E² ÷ R. Its resistance stays the same, so running it at half the voltage gives (1/2)² = 1/4 of the rated power and heat.
choice_notes: Heat goes down, not up, when the voltage is lowered on a fixed resistance.
Four times the heat would take double the voltage, not half.
With the same resistance, half the voltage gives (1/2)² = 1/4 of the power, so 1/4 as much heat.
Power depends on voltage squared, so halving the voltage cannot leave the heat the same.
final-exam-#2-052.tip_short: Heater power follows the square of the voltage (P = E² ÷ R): half the voltage gives one-quarter of the heat. Correct: C — 1/4 as much. Not A: Heat goes down, not up, when the voltage is lowered on a fixed resistance. Not B: Four times the heat would take double the voltage, not half.

final-exam-#2-053.gist: A good equipment grounding path carries a very large fault current, which makes the protective device open almost instantly. The question asks roughly how long that current flows.
final-exam-#2-053.reference_text:
Grounding and Bonding • Fault Clearing
The equipment grounding conductor gives fault current a low-impedance path so the overcurrent device opens very fast. A high fault current through a current-limiting fuse or breaker is typically cleared within about one-half cycle; 60 cycles is a full second.
choice_notes: A high fault current on a low-impedance path is typically cleared within about one-half cycle by current-limiting devices.
Six seconds would let the fault current overheat conductors and equipment; a good fault path trips far faster.
60 cycles is one full second, far longer than a device takes to clear a high-current ground fault.
120 cycles is two seconds, far longer than a device takes to clear a high-current ground fault.
final-exam-#2-053.tip_short: A low-impedance ground-fault path lets the protective device clear very high fault current within about a half cycle. Correct: A — 1/2 cycle. A high fault current on a low-impedance path is typically cleared within about one-half cycle by current-limiting devices. Not B: Six seconds would let the fault current overheat conductors and equipment; a good fault path trips far faster.

final-exam-#2-054.gist: Bends are described as fractions of a full circle. The question asks how many degrees a quarter of a circle is.
final-exam-#2-054.reference_text:
Raceway Bending • Bend Angles
A full circle is 360 degrees, so one quarter of it is 90 degrees. A quarter bend in a raceway is a 90-degree bend; the Code limits the total between pull points to 360 degrees.
choice_notes: One quarter of a full 360-degree circle is 90 degrees, so a quarter bend is a 90-degree bend.
45 degrees is one-eighth of a circle, often called an eighth bend.
25 degrees is not a quarter of a circle.
180 degrees is a half circle, two quarter bends.
final-exam-#2-054.tip_short: A quarter bend is one quarter of 360 degrees, which is a 90-degree bend. Correct: A — 90.

final-exam-#2-055.gist: Current flows through the metal of a conductor, and several properties of that metal set its resistance. The question asks which choice has nothing to do with it.
final-exam-#2-055.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Conductor Resistance
A conductor's resistance depends on its material, length, cross-sectional area (diameter), and temperature. The insulation does not carry current, so it does not change the conductor's resistance.
choice_notes: Resistance rises with length; a longer conductor has more resistance.
Resistance falls as diameter (cross-sectional area) grows.
The insulation carries no current, so it does not affect the conductor's resistance.
Resistance of copper and aluminum rises as temperature rises.
final-exam-#2-055.tip_short: Conductor resistance: material, length, diameter, and temperature matter; the insulation does not. Correct: C — Insulation of the conductor. The insulation carries no current, so it does not affect the conductor's resistance. Not A: Resistance rises with length; a longer conductor has more resistance. Not B: Resistance falls as diameter (cross-sectional area) grows.

final-exam-#2-056.gist: Coils and capacitors shift the timing between voltage and current in opposite directions. The question asks which condition makes the voltage peak first.
final-exam-#2-056.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Phase Relationship (ELI the ICE man)
In an inductive circuit, voltage (E) leads current (I): ELI. In a capacitive circuit, current leads voltage: ICE. When inductive reactance is greater than capacitive reactance, the circuit is inductive and voltage leads current.
choice_notes: When inductive reactance exceeds capacitive reactance the circuit is inductive, and voltage leads current (ELI).
Reactance exceeding resistance does not say whether it is inductive or capacitive, so it does not decide which leads.
When resistance is larger the phase angle is small, but it does not make voltage lead.
When capacitive reactance is larger the circuit is capacitive, and current leads voltage (ICE).
final-exam-#2-056.tip_short: ELI the ICE man: in an inductive (L) circuit voltage leads current; in a capacitive (C) circuit current leads voltage. Correct: A — inductive reactance exceeds the capacitive reactance. When inductive reactance exceeds capacitive reactance the circuit is inductive, and voltage leads current (ELI). Not B: Reactance exceeding resistance does not say whether it is inductive or capacitive, so it does not decide which leads. Not C: When resistance is larger the phase angle is small, but it does not make voltage lead. Not D: When capacitive reactance is larger the circuit is capacitive, and current leads voltage (ICE).

final-exam-#2-057.gist: Tape measures and drill sizes use fractions, but calculators and specs use decimals. The question asks for the decimal form of eleven sixteenths.
final-exam-#2-057.reference_text:
Trade Math • Fractions to Decimals
Divide the numerator by the denominator: 11 ÷ 16 = 0.6875. Sixteenths step by 0.0625, so 9/16 = 0.5625, 13/16 = 0.8125, and 15/16 = 0.9375.
choice_notes: 11 divided by 16 equals 0.6875.
final-exam-#2-057.tip_short: Fraction to decimal: divide the top by the bottom; each sixteenth is 0.0625. Correct: B — .6875.
final-exam-#2-057.formula: Divide the numerator by the denominator.

final-exam-#2-058.gist: Plastic conduit changes with temperature: it softens one way and stiffens the other. The informational note in the PVC uses-permitted section warns about one extreme. The question asks which one makes it brittle.
final-exam-#2-058.reference_text:
352.10 Uses Permitted
The use of PVC conduit shall be permitted in accordance with 352.10(A) through (K).
Informational Note: Extreme cold may cause some nonmetallic conduits to become brittle and, therefore, more susceptible to damage from physical contact.
choice_notes: Heat softens PVC and causes expansion; the 352.10 note warns that extreme cold causes brittleness.
The 352.10 Informational Note says extreme cold may cause some nonmetallic conduits to become brittle.
Sunlight resistance is a listing issue; the 352.10 note names extreme cold for brittleness.
PVC is permitted in wet locations by 352.10(E); moisture does not make it brittle.
final-exam-#2-058.tip_short: Cold makes PVC brittle and easy to crack on impact; heat makes it soft and expand. Correct: B — cold.

final-exam-#2-059.gist: A metal fence near a substation's exposed conductors can pick up dangerous touch voltage during a fault. The question asks the distance within which the fence must be bonded.
final-exam-#2-059.reference_text:
250.194(A) Metal Fences
If metal fences are located within 5 m (16 ft) of the exposed electrical conductors or equipment, the fence shall be bonded to the grounding electrode system with wire-type bonding jumpers as follows:
Bonding jumpers shall be installed at each fence corner and at maximum 50 m (160 ft) intervals along the fence.
choice_notes: 25 feet is not the distance in 250.194(A); fences within 16 feet must be bonded.
24 feet is not the distance in 250.194(A); fences within 16 feet must be bonded.
20 feet is not the distance in 250.194(A); fences within 16 feet must be bonded.
250.194(A) requires metal fences within 5 m (16 feet) of exposed conductors or equipment to be bonded.
final-exam-#2-059.tip_short: Substation metal fences within 16 feet of exposed conductors or equipment are bonded to the grounding electrode system at corners and at 160-foot maximum intervals. Correct: D — 16.

final-exam-#2-060.gist: Whether NM cable can be used in an apartment building depends on the building code construction type, not the number of stories. The question asks which construction types allow it.
final-exam-#2-060.reference_text:

Multi-family dwellings and their detached garages permitted to be of Types III, IV, and V construction.

Type III is one allowed type, but 334.10(2) also lists Types IV and V.
Type IV is one allowed type, but 334.10(2) also lists Types III and V.
334.10(2) permits NM cable in multifamily dwellings permitted to be of Types III, IV, and V construction.
final-exam-#2-060.tip_short: NM cable is allowed in multifamily dwellings permitted to be Types III, IV, and V construction. Correct: D — all of these. 334.10(2) permits NM cable in multifamily dwellings permitted to be of Types III, IV, and V construction.
final-exam-#2-060.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: cable, dwelling unit. Start with 334.10, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

final-exam-#2-061.prompt: When sizing a branch circuit for a fixed storage-type water heater with a capacity of 120 gallons or less, the overcurrent device and conductors must be rated at least 125 percent of the water heater rating, the same sizing used for a/an ___.

The branch-circuit over-current device and conductors for fixed storage-type water heaters that have a capacity of 450 L (120 gal) or less shall have an ampere rating of not less than 125 percent of the ampere rating of the water heater.

final-exam-#2-062.prompt: In other than one- and two-family dwelling units, the available fault current and the date the calculation was performed shall be field marked on the enclosure of ___.

final-exam-#2-062.tip_short: Outside one- and two-family dwellings, switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards are field marked with the available fault current and the calculation date. Correct: D — all of these.

final-exam-#2-063.gist: Firefighters need an outdoor switch that kills power to a one- or two-family dwelling, and a meter disconnect is one way to provide it. The question asks how that meter disconnect relates to the meter equipment.

Each disconnect shall be one of the following:

final-exam-#2-064.gist: Sometimes putting a disconnect at the motor itself is impractical or more dangerous, so the Code lets the controller's disconnect do the job if it can be secured off. The question asks the condition.

choice_notes: Serviceable is not the condition; the 430.102(B) exception requires the controller disconnect to be lockable.

The 430.102(B) exception requires the motor controller disconnecting means to be lockable in accordance with 110.25.
Readily accessible is not the condition; the 430.102(B) exception requires lockable per 110.25.

final-exam-#2-064.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: motor, disconnecting means. Start with 430.102(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

final-exam-#2-065.gist: Box fill counts each device on a yoke as if it were a number of conductors, no matter how many terminals it has. The question asks how many conductors a three-way switch counts as.

final-exam-#2-066.prompt: Equipment intended to interrupt current at fault levels shall have a/an ___ rating, at nominal circuit voltage, that is at least equal to the available fault current at the line terminals of the equipment.

final-exam-#2-067.gist: Trees sway, grow, and fall in storms, which strains anything tied to them. The question asks what the Code forbids hanging on a tree.

Boxes for an outdoor luminaire are associated equipment that 410.36(G) permits on trees.
225.26 says vegetation such as trees shall not be used for support of overhead conductor spans.
Not any of these; luminaires and associated equipment may be supported by trees (410.36(G)).
final-exam-#2-067.tip_short: Trees may carry outdoor luminaires and their equipment (410.36(G)), but never overhead conductor spans (225.26). Correct: C — overhead conductor spans.

final-exam-#2-068.gist: A light inside a commercial kitchen hood sits in the airstream pulled off the cooking surface. The question asks what else, besides grease and oil, must be kept out of its lamp and wiring compartment.
final-exam-#2-068.reference_text:
410.10(C) In Ducts or Hoods
Luminaires shall be permitted to be installed in commercial cooking hoods where all of the following conditions are met:
(2) The luminaire shall be constructed so that all exhaust vapors, grease, oil, or cooking vapors are excluded from the lamp and wiring compartment. Diffusers shall be resistant to thermal shock.
choice_notes: Solids are not named in 410.10(C)(2); the luminaire must exclude exhaust vapors, grease, oil, and cooking vapors.
Moisture is not in the 410.10(C)(2) list; it names exhaust vapors, grease, oil, and cooking vapors.
Oxygen cannot practically be excluded and is not in the 410.10(C)(2) list.
410.10(C)(2) requires all exhaust vapors, grease, oil, or cooking vapors to be excluded from the lamp and wiring compartment.
final-exam-#2-068.tip_short: Hood luminaires (410.10(C)): identified for the use, sealed against exhaust vapors, grease, oil, and cooking vapors, corrosion resistant and smooth, with no wiring exposed in the hood. Correct: D — exhaust vapors.

final-exam-#2-069.gist: Two different metals touching in a wet or chemical setting can corrode each other through galvanic action. The question asks the condition under which stainless RMC may still be used with galvanized boxes.
final-exam-#2-069.reference_text:
344.14 Dissimilar Metals
Where practicable, dissimilar metals in contact anywhere in the system shall be avoided to eliminate the possibility of galvanic action. Stainless steel and aluminum fittings and enclosures shall be permitted to be used with galvanized steel RMC, and galvanized steel fittings and enclosures shall be permitted to be used with aluminum RMC where not subject to severe corrosive influences. Stainless steel rigid conduit shall only be used with the following:
(1) Stainless steel fittings
(2) Stainless steel boxes and enclosures
(3) Steel (galvanized, painted, powder or PVC coated, and so forth) boxes and enclosures when not subject to severe corrosive influences
(4) Stainless steel, nonmetallic, or approved accessories
choice_notes: 344.14(3) permits galvanized steel boxes and enclosures with stainless steel RMC when not subject to severe corrosive influences.
Unauthorized contact is a guarding concern, not the dissimilar metals limit of 344.14.
344.14 limits the mix only where influences are severe, not where there are any corrosive influences at all.
Physical damage is a separate protection concern; 344.14 is about corrosion from dissimilar metals.
final-exam-#2-069.tip_short: Stainless RMC (344.14) mixes with galvanized or coated steel boxes only where there are no severe corrosive influences. Correct: A — severe corrosive influences.

final-exam-#2-070.gist: Flexible metallic tubing is a light, liquidtight tubing meant for short runs in dry, accessible places. The question asks the largest trade size made for it.
final-exam-#2-070.reference_text:
360.20(B) Maximum
The maximum size of FMT shall be metric designator 21 (trade size 3/4).
choice_notes: Trade size 1/2 is the minimum size of FMT in 360.20(A), not the maximum.
360.20(B) limits FMT to metric designator 21, trade size 3/4.
Trade size 1 is larger than the 360.20(B) maximum of trade size 3/4.
Trade size 1 1/4 is larger than the 360.20(B) maximum of trade size 3/4.
final-exam-#2-070.tip_short: FMT (360.20): trade size 1/2 minimum (3/8 in some uses), trade size 3/4 maximum. Correct: B — 3/4". 360.20(B) limits FMT to metric designator 21, trade size 3/4. Not A: Trade size 1/2 is the minimum size of FMT in 360.20(A), not the maximum. Not C: Trade size 1 is larger than the 360.20(B) maximum of trade size 3/4. Not D: Trade size 1 1/4 is larger than the 360.20(B) maximum of trade size 3/4.

final-exam-#4-001.gist: Commercial kitchen demand factors can cut the calculated load a lot when there are many units. The question asks what floor the Code puts under that reduced load.
final-exam-#4-001.reference_text:
220.56 Kitchen Equipment - Other Than Dwelling Unit(s)
Calculating the load for commercial electric cooking equipment, dishwasher booster heaters, water heaters, and other kitchen equipment in accordance with Table 220.56 shall be permitted. Other kitchen equipment shall include equipment that is fastened in place and rated 1/4 hp or greater, or 500 watts or greater. These demand factors shall be applied to all equipment that has either thermostatic control or intermittent use as kitchen equipment. These demand factors shall not apply to space-heating, ventilating, or air-conditioning equipment.
However, in no case shall the feeder or service calculated load be less than the sum of the largest two kitchen equipment loads.
choice_notes: 220.56 sets the floor: the feeder or service load can never be less than the sum of the largest two kitchen equipment loads.
220.56 says its demand factors do not apply to space-heating, ventilating, or air-conditioning equipment at all.
The full rating of all appliances would cancel the demand factors; the floor is only the two largest kitchen loads.
Receptacle loads are calculated under 220.14 and 220.44, not as the minimum for Table 220.56 kitchen equipment.
final-exam-#4-001.tip_short: Commercial kitchen equipment (220.56): Table 220.56 demand factors apply, but the result can never drop below the two biggest kitchen loads added together. Correct: A — largest two kitchen equipment loads. Not B: 220.56 says its demand factors do not apply to space-heating, ventilating, or air-conditioning equipment at all. Not C: The full rating of all appliances would cancel the demand factors; the floor is only the two largest kitchen loads. Not D: Receptacle loads are calculated under 220.14 and 220.44, not as the minimum for Table 220.56 kitchen equipment.

final-exam-#4-002.gist: Capacitors draw more than their rated current because of voltage and manufacturing tolerances and harmonics. The question asks the minimum conductor ampacity as a percentage of the capacitor's rated current.
final-exam-#4-002.reference_text:
460.8 Conductors
(A) Ampacity
The ampacity of capacitor circuit conductors shall not be less than 135 percent of the rated current of the capacitor. The ampacity of conductors that connect a capacitor to the terminals of a motor or to motor circuit conductors shall not be less than one-third the ampacity of the motor circuit conductors and in no case less than 135 percent of the rated current of the capacitor.
choice_notes: 80 percent is less than the rated current; 460.8(A) requires 135 percent of the capacitor's rated current.
100 percent leaves no margin; 460.8(A) requires 135 percent of the capacitor's rated current.
125 percent is the continuous-load and motor factor; capacitor conductors take 135 percent under 460.8(A).
460.8(A) requires capacitor circuit conductors of at least 135 percent of the capacitor's rated current.
final-exam-#4-002.tip_short: Capacitor conductors (460.8(A)): at least 135 percent of the capacitor's rated current, and at least one-third of the motor conductor ampacity when tied to motor terminals. Correct: D — 135%. 460.8(A) requires capacitor circuit conductors of at least 135 percent of the capacitor's rated current. Not A: 80 percent is less than the rated current; 460.8(A) requires 135 percent of the capacitor's rated current. Not B: 100 percent leaves no margin; 460.8(A) requires 135 percent of the capacitor's rated current. Not C: 125 percent is the continuous-load and motor factor; capacitor conductors take 135 percent under 460.8(A).

final-exam-#4-003.gist: Every raceway article has a section limiting how full the raceway can be. The question asks which Chapter 9 table sets that limit for liquidtight flexible nonmetallic conduit.
final-exam-#4-003.reference_text:
356.22 Number of Conductors
The number of conductors shall not exceed that permitted by the percentage fill specified in Table 1, Chapter 9.
choice_notes: Chapter 9 has no Table 7; the fill percentages for LFNC come from Table 1.
Informative Annex D contains calculation examples, not the fill limits for LFNC.
356.22 limits LFNC to the percentage fill specified in Table 1, Chapter 9.
Table 4 gives the conduit areas used in the arithmetic; the permitted fill percentage is set by Table 1.
final-exam-#4-003.tip_short: Raceway fill: each raceway article (for LFNC, 356.22) points to Chapter 9, Table 1 for the fill percentage (53, 31, or 40 percent). Correct: C — Table 1. Not B: Informative Annex D contains calculation examples, not the fill limits for LFNC.

final-exam-#4-004.gist: Outside dwellings, each receptacle yoke counts as a load in the calculation. The question asks at what size a multiple-receptacle assembly switches to the reduced per-receptacle figure.
final-exam-#4-004.reference_text:
220.14 Other Loads - All Occupancies
(I) Receptacle Outlets
Except as covered in 220.41 and 220.14(J), receptacle outlets shall be calculated at not less than 180 volt-amperes for each single or for each multiple receptacle on one yoke. A single piece of equipment consisting of a multiple receptacle comprised of four or more receptacles shall be calculated at not less than 90 volt-amperes per receptacle. This provision shall not be applicable to the receptacle outlets specified in 210.11(C)(1) and (C)(2).
choice_notes: One receptacle on a yoke is calculated at 180 VA under 220.14(I); the 90 VA rate needs four or more.
Two receptacles on one yoke still count 180 VA; the 90 VA per receptacle rate needs four or more.
Three receptacles do not reach the threshold; 220.14(I) applies 90 VA per receptacle at four or more.
220.14(I): a single piece of equipment with four or more receptacles is calculated at not less than 90 VA per receptacle.
final-exam-#4-004.tip_short: Receptacle loads (220.14(I)): 180 VA per single or multiple receptacle on one yoke; one piece of equipment with four or more receptacles counts 90 VA per receptacle. Correct: D — four.

final-exam-#4-005.gist: Standard metal boxes that are not marked have their volume listed in the box table by trade size. The question asks the listed volume for this device box.
final-exam-#4-005.reference_text:
Table 314.16(A) Metal Boxes
Box Trade Size	Minimum Volume	Maximum Number of Conductors* (arranged by AWG size)
mm	in.	 	cm3	in.3	18	16	14	12	10	8	6
75 × 50 × 38	(3 × 2 × 11/2)	device	123	7.5	5	4	3	3	3	2	1
75 × 50 × 50	(3 × 2 × 2)	device	164	10.0	6	5	5	4	4	3	2
75 × 50 × 57	(3 × 2 × 21/4)	device	172	10.5	7	6	5	4	4	3	2
choice_notes: Table 314.16(A) lists the 3 x 2 x 2 in. device box at 10.0 cubic inches.
12 cubic inches is not a listed device box volume; the 3 x 2 x 2 in. box is 10.0 cubic inches.

final-exam-#4-006.gist: Voltage-drop work uses the resistance and impedance of conductors per unit length, which depend on the metal and the raceway. The question asks the per-1,000-foot figure for large aluminum wire in steel.
choice_notes: 0.052 ohms is the reactance (XL) of 4/0 in steel conduit per 1000 feet, not the aluminum resistance or impedance.
0.0102 ohms is ten times too small for 4/0 aluminum per 1000 feet.
0.1012 ohms matches no Table 9 entry; 4/0 aluminum in steel conduit is 0.11 ohms per 1000 feet.
NEC 2023 Table 9 gives 4/0 aluminum in steel conduit 0.11 ohms to neutral per 1000 feet, for both AC resistance and effective Z at 0.85 PF.
final-exam-#4-006.tip_short: Chapter 9, Table 9: each size has two rows, ohms per kilometer then ohms per 1000 feet; pick the aluminum and the steel conduit columns. Correct: D — 0.11.
final-exam-#4-006.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: raceway. Start with Table 9, Chapter 9, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

final-exam-#4-007.gist: A system called 120/240 may actually measure a few volts higher or lower. The question asks the Article 100 term for the class name given to it.
final-exam-#4-007.reference_text:
Article 100 Definitions
Voltage, Nominal. (Nominal Voltage) A nominal value assigned to a circuit or system for the purpose of conveniently designating its voltage class (e.g., 120/240 volts, 480Y/277 volts, 600 volts). (CMP—1)
Informational Note No. 1: The actual voltage at which a circuit operates can vary from the nominal within a range that permits satisfactory operation of equipment.
choice_notes: An average voltage is a measured quantity, not the Article 100 term for a voltage class designation.
Source voltage is not an Article 100 defined term for designating a voltage class.
Article 100 defines nominal voltage as a value assigned to designate a circuit's voltage class, such as 120/240 volts.
Effective (RMS) voltage is a measurement of an AC waveform, not the class designation defined in Article 100.
final-exam-#4-007.tip_short: Article 100 voltage terms: nominal is the class name (120/240, 480Y/277); the actual operating voltage may vary from it within a range. Correct: C — nominal.

final-exam-#4-008.gist: Sizing a room air conditioner's circuit is simpler when the Code lets you treat it as one motor. The question asks the current limit for that treatment.
final-exam-#4-008.reference_text:
440.62 Branch-Circuit Requirements
(A) Room Air Conditioner as a Single Motor Unit
A room air conditioner shall be considered as a single motor unit in determining its branch-circuit requirements where all the following conditions are met:
It is cord- and attachment-plug-connected.
Its rating is not more than 40 amperes and 250 volts, single phase.
choice_notes: 20 amperes is below the limit; 440.62(A)(2) allows the single motor unit treatment up to 40 amperes.
25 amperes is below the limit; 440.62(A)(2) allows up to 40 amperes at 250 volts single-phase.
30 amperes is below the limit; 440.62(A)(2) allows up to 40 amperes at 250 volts single-phase.
440.62(A)(2): the rating is not more than 40 amperes and 250 volts, single phase.
final-exam-#4-008.tip_short: Room air conditioners (440.62(A)): treated as a single motor unit when cord-and-plug connected, rated not over 40 A and 250 V single-phase, with total rated-load current on the nameplate. Correct: D — 40 amps. 440.62(A)(2): the rating is not more than 40 amperes and 250 volts, single phase. Not A: 20 amperes is below the limit; 440.62(A)(2) allows the single motor unit treatment up to 40 amperes. Not B: 25 amperes is below the limit; 440.62(A)(2) allows up to 40 amperes at 250 volts single-phase. Not C: 30 amperes is below the limit; 440.62(A)(2) allows up to 40 amperes at 250 volts single-phase.
final-exam-#4-008.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: motor. Start with 440.62(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

final-exam-#4-009.gist: A metal cable tray can serve as the equipment grounding conductor only if it has enough metal for the protective device ahead of it. The question asks the largest breaker this tray's metal area supports.
final-exam-#4-009.reference_text:
Table 392.60(B) Metal Area Requirements for Cable Trays Used as Equipment Grounding Conductor
Maximum Fuse Ampere Rating, Circuit Breaker Ampere Trip Setting, or Circuit Breaker Protective Relay Ampere Trip Setting for Ground-Fault Protection of Any Cable Circuit in the Cable Tray System	Minimum Cross-Sectional Area of Metal*
†Steel cable trays shall not be used as equipment grounding conductors for circuits with ground-fault protection above 600 amperes. Aluminum cable trays shall not be used as equipment grounding conductors for circuits with ground-fault protection above 2000 amperes.
reference_table: NOTE: Table 392.60(B). Steel trays may not serve as the equipment grounding conductor above 600 A.
choice_notes: 1000 amperes is listed only for aluminum trays; steel trays may not be used above 600 amperes.
600 amperes requires 1.50 square inches of steel; 0.79 square inches does not qualify.
0.79 square inches meets the 0.70 square inch steel row (200 A) but not the 1.00 square inch row, so 200 A is the maximum.
400 amperes requires 1.00 square inch of steel; 0.79 square inches falls short.
final-exam-#4-009.tip_short: Table 392.60(B): find the smallest required metal area that the tray meets or exceeds; you may not round up to the next row. Correct: C — 200.

final-exam-#4-010.gist: Bathroom receptacle rules are not based on countertop length the way kitchen rules are. The question asks how many are required for this single-sink counter.
final-exam-#4-010.reference_text:
210.52 Dwelling Unit Receptacle Outlets
(D) Bathrooms
At least one receptacle outlet shall be installed in bathrooms within 900 mm (3 ft) of the outside edge of each sink. The receptacle outlet shall be located on a wall or partition that is adjacent to the sink or sink countertop, located on the countertop, or installed on the side or face of the sink cabinet. In no case shall the receptacle be located more than 300 mm (12 in.) below the top of the sink or sink countertop. Receptacle outlet assemblies listed for use in countertops shall be permitted to be installed in the countertop.
choice_notes: 210.52(D) requires at least one receptacle within 3 ft of each sink; one sink needs one receptacle.
Three receptacles would apply kitchen spacing; bathrooms need one within 3 ft of each sink.
Four receptacles has no basis; one sink needs one receptacle outlet under 210.52(D).
A dwelling bathroom must have at least one receptacle outlet within 3 ft of each sink.
final-exam-#4-010.tip_short: Bathroom receptacles (210.52(D)): at least one within 3 ft of the outside edge of each sink; counter length does not add receptacles as it does in kitchens. Correct: A — 1. Not C: Four receptacles has no basis; one sink needs one receptacle outlet under 210.52(D). Not D: A dwelling bathroom must have at least one receptacle outlet within 3 ft of each sink.

final-exam-#4-011.gist: The box you pick must be at least as big as the volume the fill calculation needs. The question asks the smallest listed device box that holds this much.
final-exam-#4-011.reference_text:
Table 314.16(A) Metal Boxes
Box Trade Size	Minimum Volume	Maximum Number of Conductors* (arranged by AWG size)
mm	in.	 	cm3	in.3	18	16	14	12	10	8	6
75 × 50 × 38	(3 × 2 × 11/2)	device	123	7.5	5	4	3	3	3	2	1
75 × 50 × 50	(3 × 2 × 2)	device	164	10.0	6	5	5	4	4	3	2
75 × 50 × 57	(3 × 2 × 21/4)	device	172	10.5	7	6	5	4	4	3	2

The 3 x 2 x 2-1/4 in. device box is 10.5 cubic inches, the smallest listed box of at least 10.25.
The 3 x 2 x 2 in. device box is 10.0 cubic inches, less than the 10.25 required.
A 2 x 3 x 3 in. box is not a Table 314.16(A) device box size.
final-exam-#4-011.tip_short: Picking a box: the Table 314.16(A) volume must equal or exceed the required fill; choose the first listed box at or above it. Correct: B — 3" x 2" x 2 1/4". The 3 x 2 x 2-1/4 in. device box is 10.5 cubic inches, the smallest listed box of at least 10.25. Not A: A 2 x 2 x 3 in. box is not a Table 314.16(A) device box size. final-exam-#4-012.gist: Show windows are lit intensely, so the Code sets a load per foot of window rather than per outlet. The question asks that figure.
final-exam-#4-012.reference_text:
220.14 Other Loads - All Occupancies
(G) Show Windows
Show windows shall be calculated in accordance with either of the following:
The unit load per outlet as required in other provisions of this section
At 200 volt-amperes per linear 300 mm (1 ft) of show window
choice_notes: 180 VA is the load for each general receptacle outlet under 220.14(I), not for show windows.
1500 VA is the small-appliance and laundry circuit load of 220.52, not a show window load.
1800 VA is not a Code per-foot load; it is the capacity of a 15-ampere, 120-volt circuit.
220.14(G)(2) calculates show windows at 200 volt-amperes per linear foot.
final-exam-#4-012.tip_short: Show windows (220.14(G), 220.46(A)): calculate per linear foot of window measured along its base, or per outlet, whichever the section allows. Correct: D — 200.
final-exam-#4-012.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 220.14(G), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

final-exam-#4-013.gist: Cord-and-plug-connected office partitions share one supply, so the Code limits how many receptacles they can carry. The question asks that limit.
final-exam-#4-013.reference_text:
605.9 Freestanding-Type Office Furnishings, Cord- And Plug-Connected
(C) Receptacle. Maximum
An individual office furnishing or groups of interconnected individual office furnishings shall not contain more than 13 15-ampere, 125-volt receptacles. For purposes of this requirement, a receptacle is considered (1) up to two (simplex) receptacles provided within a single enclosure and that are within 0.3 m (1 ft) of each other or (2) one duplex receptacle.
choice_notes: 10 is below the limit; 605.9(C) permits up to 13 receptacles.
605.9(C) permits no more than thirteen 15-ampere, 125-volt receptacles in the furnishing or group.
12 is below the limit; 605.9(C) permits up to 13 receptacles.
6 is below the limit; 605.9(C) permits up to 13 receptacles.
final-exam-#4-013.tip_short: Freestanding office furnishings (605.9(C)): one furnishing or a connected group may have no more than thirteen 15-ampere, 125-volt receptacles. Correct: B — 13. 605.9(C) permits no more than thirteen 15-ampere, 125-volt receptacles in the furnishing or group.

final-exam-#4-014.gist: Small motors can share one branch circuit if the circuit is small enough. The question asks the largest overcurrent device allowed on a 120-volt circuit for this.
final-exam-#4-014.reference_text:
430.53 Several Motors or Loads on One Branch Circuit
(A) Not Over 1 Horsepower
Several motors, each not exceeding 1 hp in rating, shall be permitted on a nominal 120-volt branch circuit protected at not over 20 amperes or a branch circuit of 1000 volts, nominal, or less, protected at not over 15 amperes, if all of the following conditions are met:
choice_notes: 15 amperes is the limit for circuits other than 120 volts; a nominal 120-volt circuit may be protected at up to 20 amperes.
430.53(A) permits a nominal 120-volt branch circuit protected at not over 20 amperes.
30 amperes exceeds the 20 ampere limit of 430.53(A).
40 amperes exceeds the 20 ampere limit of 430.53(A).
final-exam-#4-014.tip_short: Several small motors (430.53(A)): each 1 hp or less and 6 A or less; 120-volt circuits protected at not over 20 A, other circuits to 1000 V at not over 15 A. Correct: B — 20.

final-exam-#4-015.gist: The outdoor receptacle rules are part of the dwelling receptacle section. The question asks which occupancy needs one at both the front and the back.
final-exam-#4-015.reference_text:
210.52 Dwelling Unit Receptacle Outlets
(E) Outdoor Outlets
(1) One-Family and Two-Family Dwellings
For a one-family dwelling and each unit of a two-family dwelling that is at grade level, at least one receptacle outlet readily accessible from grade and not more than 2.0 m (61/2 ft) above grade level shall be installed at the front and back of the dwelling.
choice_notes: Commercial buildings are not covered by 210.52, which applies to dwelling units.
Office buildings are not dwelling units; 210.52(E)(1) applies to one- and two-family dwellings.
Motels are guest rooms, not one- or two-family dwellings, so 210.52(E)(1) does not apply.
210.52(E)(1) requires a front and back outdoor receptacle for one-family dwellings and each grade-level unit of a two-family dwelling.
final-exam-#4-015.tip_short: Outdoor receptacles (210.52(E)): one-family and each grade-level unit of a two-family dwelling need one at the front and back, readily accessible from grade and not over 6-1/2 ft up. Correct: D — one and two family dwellings. 210.52(E)(1) requires a front and back outdoor receptacle for one-family dwellings and each grade-level unit of a two-family dwelling. Not B: Office buildings are not dwelling units; 210.52(E)(1) applies to one- and two-family dwellings.

final-exam-#4-016.gist: The kitchen and dining small-appliance circuits are reserved for those rooms, with a few narrow exceptions. The question asks which listed outlet fits an exception.
final-exam-#4-016.reference_text:
210.52 Dwelling Unit Receptacle Outlets
(B) Small Appliances
(2) No Other Outlets
The two or more small-appliance branch circuits specified in 210.52(B)(1) shall have no other outlets.
Exception No. 1: A receptacle installed solely for the electrical supply to and support of an electric clock in any of the rooms specified in 210.52(B)(1) shall be permitted to be served by a small-appliance branch circuit.
choice_notes: Outdoor receptacles are other outlets; 210.52(B)(2) bars them from small-appliance circuits.
210.52(B)(2) Exception No. 1 permits a receptacle solely for an electric clock in one of those rooms.
A hallway receptacle is outside the rooms served; distance from the kitchen does not make it permitted.
A garage door opener receptacle is another outlet outside the rooms served, so it is not permitted.
final-exam-#4-016.tip_short: Small-appliance circuits (210.52(B)(2)): no other outlets, except a clock receptacle in those rooms, gas-appliance igniter outlets, and similar listed exceptions. Correct: B — Electric clock in a dining room. 210.52(B)(2) Exception No. 1 permits a receptacle solely for an electric clock in one of those rooms. Not A: Outdoor receptacles are other outlets; 210.52(B)(2) bars them from small-appliance circuits. Not C: A hallway receptacle is outside the rooms served; distance from the kitchen does not make it permitted. Not D: A garage door opener receptacle is another outlet outside the rooms served, so it is not permitted.
final-exam-#4-016.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: branch circuit, receptacle outlet. Start with 210.52(B)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

final-exam-#4-017.gist: Conductor ampacities rarely line up with breaker sizes, so the Code allows rounding up in some cases. The question asks the ceiling on that rounding up.
final-exam-#4-017.reference_text:
240.4 Protection of Conductors
(B) Overcurrent Devices Rated 800 Amperes or Less
The next higher standard overcurrent device rating (above the ampacity of the conductors being protected) shall be permitted to be used, provided all of the following conditions are met:
The conductors being protected are not part of a branch circuit supplying more than one receptacle for cord-and-plug-connected portable loads.
The ampacity of the conductors does not correspond with the standard ampere rating of a fuse or a circuit breaker without overload trip adjustments above its rating (but that shall be permitted to have other trip or rating adjustments).
The next higher standard rating selected does not exceed 800 amperes.
choice_notes: 600 amperes is not the limit; 240.4(B)(3) allows rounding up to a standard rating not over 800 amperes.
240.4(B)(3): the next higher standard rating selected must not exceed 800 amperes.
Above 800 amperes, 240.4(C) requires the device rating to not exceed the conductor ampacity.
1,200 amperes is above the 800 ampere limit; no rounding up is permitted there.
final-exam-#4-017.tip_short: Next size up (240.4(B)): allowed when the conductors do not feed multiple receptacles for portable loads and the next standard rating is not over 800 A; above that, 240.4(C) applies. Correct: B — 800. Not C: Above 800 amperes, 240.4(C) requires the device rating to not exceed the conductor ampacity.
final-exam-#4-017.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: switch ampere rating, ampacity. Start with 240.4(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

final-exam-#4-018.gist: Water lowers body resistance, so control circuits people might touch while wet must stay at low voltage. The question asks the limit for continuous DC.

522.28 Control Circuits in Wet Locations

final-exam-#4-019.gist: Dwelling appliances fastened in place get a reduced demand when there are several, but some appliance types have their own rules. The question asks which listed ones qualify.
final-exam-#4-019.reference_text:
220.53 Appliance Load - Dwelling Unit(s)
Applying a demand factor of 75 percent to the nameplate rating load of four or more appliances rated 1/4 hp or greater, or 500 watts or greater, that are fastened in place, and that are served by the same feeder or service in a one-family, two-family, or multifamily dwelling shall be permitted. This demand factor shall not apply to the following:
Household electric cooking equipment that is fastened in place
Clothes dryers
Space heating equipment
Air-conditioning equipment
Electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE)
choice_notes: Water heaters qualify, but so do dishwashers; both are fastened-in-place appliances covered by 220.53.
Dishwashers qualify, but so do water heaters under 220.53.
Water heaters and dishwashers qualify; 220.53 excludes clothes dryers, which use Table 220.54.
Clothes dryers are excluded from 220.53 and are calculated with 220.54 instead.
final-exam-#4-019.tip_short: Fastened-in-place appliances (220.53): 75 percent for four or more, excluding cooking equipment, dryers, space heating, air conditioning, and EVSE, which have their own rules. Correct: C — I and II only. Water heaters and dishwashers qualify; 220.53 excludes clothes dryers, which use Table 220.54. Not A: Water heaters qualify, but so do dishwashers; both are fastened-in-place appliances covered by 220.53. Not B: Dishwashers qualify, but so do water heaters under 220.53. Not D: Clothes dryers are excluded from 220.53 and are calculated with 220.54 instead.

final-exam-#4-020.gist: A circuit may pass through places with different conditions, giving different ampacities along its length. The question asks which one governs.
final-exam-#4-020.reference_text:
310.14 Ampacities for Conductors Rated 0 Volts — 2000 Volts
(A) General
(2) Selection of Ampacity
Where more than one ampacity applies for a given circuit length, the lowest value shall be used.
Exception: Where different ampacities apply to portions of a circuit, the higher ampacity shall be permitted to be used if the total portion(s) of the circuit with lower ampacity does not exceed the lesser of 3.0 m (10 ft) or 10 percent of the total circuit.
choice_notes: 310.14(A)(2) requires the lowest value where more than one ampacity applies for a given circuit length.
Averaging ampacities is not permitted; the weakest section would overheat.
The highest value is allowed only under the exception, for a short lower-ampacity portion; otherwise the lowest applies.
One of the listed choices is correct: 310.14(A)(2) requires the lowest value.
final-exam-#4-020.tip_short: Ampacity along a run (310.14(A)(2)): the lowest applies, unless the lower-ampacity portion is no longer than 10 ft or 10 percent of the circuit. Correct: A — lowest. Not B: Averaging ampacities is not permitted; the weakest section would overheat. Not D: One of the listed choices is correct: 310.14(A)(2) requires the lowest value.

220.5 Calculations
(C) Floor Area
The floor area for each floor shall be calculated from the outside dimensions of the building, dwelling unit, or other area involved. For dwelling units, the calculated floor area shall not include open porches or unfinished areas not adaptable for future use as a habitable room or occupiable space.
220.41 Dwelling Units, Minimum Unit Load
In one-family, two-family, and multifamily dwellings, the minimum unit load shall be not less than 33 volt-amperes/m2 (3 volt-amperes/ft2).
choice_notes: 2000 square feet of living area x 3 VA per square foot = 6000 VA.
6600 VA counts all 2200 square feet under the roof, including space 220.5(C) leaves out.
