final-exam-#4-027.tip_short: Dwelling lighting load: 3 VA per square foot (220.41) of floor area from outside dimensions, leaving out open porches and unfinished spaces not adaptable for future use (220.5(C)). Correct: A — 6000.
final-exam-#4-027.formula: Floor area counted under 220.5(C) × the 220.41 dwelling unit load.

final-exam-#4-028.gist: A dwelling needs at least two small-appliance circuits and one laundry circuit, and each has a fixed calculated load. The question asks their combined minimum.
final-exam-#4-028.reference_text:
220.52 Small-Appliance and Laundry Loads - Dwelling Unit
(A) Small-Appliance Circuit Load
In each dwelling unit, the load shall be calculated at 1500 volt-amperes for each 2-wire small-appliance branch circuit as covered by 210.11(C)(1). Where the load is subdivided through two or more feeders, the calculated load for each shall include not less than 1500 volt-amperes for each 2-wire small-appliance branch circuit. These loads shall be permitted to be included with the general lighting load and subjected to the demand factors provided in Table 220.45.
(B) Laundry Circuit Load
A load of not less than 1500 volt-amperes shall be included for each 2-wire laundry branch circuit installed as covered by 210.11(C)(2). This load shall be permitted to be included with the general lighting load and shall be subjected to the demand factors provided in Table 220.45.

3000 VA covers only the two small-appliance circuits and leaves out the laundry circuit.
Two small-appliance circuits at 1500 VA plus one laundry circuit at 1500 VA = 4500 VA.
6000 VA counts four circuits; the minimum is two small-appliance circuits and one laundry circuit.

open-book-exam-#11-001.gist: A balcony, deck, or porch attached to or very close to a dwelling needs its own outdoor receptacle outlet. The question asks how close, horizontally, the structure must be for the rule to apply.
open-book-exam-#11-001.reference_text:
210.52(E)(3) Balconies, Decks, and Porches
Balconies, decks, and porches that are within 102 mm (4 in.) horizontally of the dwelling unit shall have at least one receptacle outlet accessible from the balcony, deck, or porch. The receptacle outlet shall not be located more than 2.0 m (61/2 ft) above the balcony, deck, or porch walking surface.
choice_notes: 210.52(E)(3) applies to balconies, decks, and porches within 102 mm (4 inches) horizontally of the dwelling unit.
6 inches is not the distance in 210.52(E)(3); the trigger is within 4 inches horizontally.
12 inches is not the trigger; 210.52(E)(3) applies within 4 inches of the dwelling unit.
18 inches is not the trigger; 210.52(E)(3) applies within 4 inches of the dwelling unit.
open-book-exam-#11-001.tip_short: Balconies, decks, and porches within 4 inches of the dwelling need a receptacle outlet no higher than 6 1/2 feet above the walking surface. Correct: A — 4.

open-book-exam-#11-002.gist: An open breaker space in a panel exposes live bus, so it must be filled with a proper blank. The question asks which defined term describes the required closures.
open-book-exam-#11-002.reference_text:
408.7 Unused Openings
Unused openings for circuit breakers and switches shall be closed using identified closures, or other approved means that provide protection substantially equivalent to the wall of the enclosure.
choice_notes: Approved applies to the other means in 408.7; the closures themselves must be identified.
408.7 requires unused openings to be closed using identified closures.
Labeled is not the term in 408.7; the closures must be identified for the purpose.
Marked is not the term in 408.7; the closures must be identified for the purpose.
open-book-exam-#11-002.tip_short: Open breaker spaces in a panelboard get identified filler plates (or other approved means equal to the enclosure wall). Correct: B — identified.

open-book-exam-#11-003.gist: The NEC has a general word for any place where equipment gets its power from the wiring, whether a receptacle or a hard-wired light. The question asks that defined term.
open-book-exam-#11-003.reference_text:
Article 100 Definitions — Outlet
Outlet. A point on the wiring system at which current is taken to supply utilization equipment. (CMP—1)
choice_notes: Article 100 defines an outlet as a point on the wiring system at which current is taken to supply utilization equipment.
A receptacle is a contact device for an attachment plug; it is one type of outlet, not the definition.
A junction is where conductors are joined, not where current is taken to supply equipment.
Dead end is not an NEC defined term for a point supplying utilization equipment.
open-book-exam-#11-003.tip_short: An outlet is any point where current is taken to supply utilization equipment; a receptacle is only one kind of outlet. Correct: A — outlet.
open-book-exam-#11-003.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: receptacle outlet. Start with Article 100, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#11-004.gist: Homes have lamps and fixtures handled by people with no electrical training, so the Code limits the voltage at luminaire terminals there. The question asks that limit.
open-book-exam-#11-004.reference_text:
210.6(A) Occupancy Limitation
In dwelling units and guest rooms or guest suites of hotels, motels, and similar occupancies, the voltage shall not exceed 120 volts, nominal, between conductors that supply the terminals of the following:
Luminaires
Cord-and-plug-connected loads 1440 volt-amperes, nominal, or less or less than 1/4 hp
choice_notes: 210.6(A) limits the voltage between conductors supplying luminaire terminals in dwelling units to 120 volts, nominal.
220 volts exceeds the 210.6(A) limit of 120 volts for dwelling unit luminaires.
230 volts exceeds the 210.6(A) limit of 120 volts for dwelling unit luminaires.
240 volts is common in homes for appliances, but 210.6(A) limits luminaires to 120 volts.
open-book-exam-#11-004.tip_short: Dwelling units and hotel guest rooms: 120 volts maximum between conductors supplying luminaires and small cord-and-plug loads. Correct: A — 120.

open-book-exam-#11-005.gist: Plastic conduit changes with temperature: it softens one way and stiffens the other. The informational note in the PVC uses-permitted section warns about one extreme. The question asks which one makes it brittle.
open-book-exam-#11-005.reference_text:
352.10 Uses Permitted
The use of PVC conduit shall be permitted in accordance with 352.10(A) through (K).
Informational Note: Extreme cold may cause some nonmetallic conduits to become brittle and, therefore, more susceptible to damage from physical contact.
choice_notes: Heat softens PVC and causes expansion; the 352.10 note warns that extreme cold causes brittleness.
The 352.10 Informational Note says extreme cold may cause some nonmetallic conduits to become brittle.
Sunlight resistance is a listing issue; the 352.10 note names extreme cold for brittleness.
PVC is permitted in wet locations by 352.10(E); moisture does not make it brittle.
open-book-exam-#11-005.tip_short: Cold makes PVC brittle and easy to crack on impact; heat makes it soft and expand. Correct: B — cold.
open-book-exam-#11-005.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: conduit. Start with 352.10, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#11-006.gist: One GFCI on a feeder can protect every branch circuit downstream, but it has to be reachable for testing and resetting. The question asks the access level required.
open-book-exam-#11-006.reference_text:
215.9 Ground-Fault Circuit-Interrupter Protection for Personnel
Feeders shall be permitted to be protected by a listed ground-fault circuit interrupter installed in a readily accessible location in lieu of the provisions for such interrupters as specified in 210.8 and 590.6(A).

open-book-exam-#11-006.tip_short: A feeder GFCI may replace branch-circuit GFCIs if it is listed and installed in a readily accessible location. Correct: B — readily accessible.

If metal fences are located within 5 m (16 ft) of the exposed electrical conductors or equipment, the fence shall be bonded to the grounding electrode system with wire-type bonding jumpers as follows:
Bonding jumpers shall be installed at each fence corner and at maximum 50 m (160 ft) intervals along the fence.

open-book-exam-#11-011.prompt: Power distribution blocks installed on ___ conductors shall be marked as suitable for use on the line side of the main disconnecting equipment, or equivalent.

open-book-exam-#11-011.reference_text:

Service-entrance conductors shall be permitted to be spliced or tapped in accordance with 110.14, 300.5(E), 300.13, and 300.15. The factory cannot know the installed protective device; 700.5(F) requires a field marking.
700.5(F) does not give a choice; the rating shall be field marked.
700.5(F) requires only a field marking of the short-circuit current rating, not both.
open-book-exam-#11-013.tip_short: Emergency transfer equipment: the short-circuit current rating, based on the actual protective device, is field marked on the exterior. Correct: A — field marked. Not B: The factory cannot know the installed protective device; 700.5(F) requires a field marking. Not C: 700.5(F) does not give a choice; the rating shall be field marked. Not D: 700.5(F) requires only a field marking of the short-circuit current rating, not both.

open-book-exam-#11-014.prompt: When sizing a branch circuit for a fixed storage-type water heater with a capacity of 120 gallons or less, the overcurrent device and conductors must be rated at least 125 percent of the water heater rating, the same sizing used for a/an ___.
open-book-exam-#11-014.gist: A tank water heater can run for hours to recover after heavy use, so its branch circuit gets the same extra margin as other long-running loads. The question asks which kind of load that sizing matches.
open-book-exam-#11-014.reference_text:
422.13 Storage-Type Water Heaters
The branch-circuit over-current device and conductors for fixed storage-type water heaters that have a capacity of 450 L (120 gal) or less shall have an ampere rating of not less than 125 percent of the ampere rating of the water heater.
choice_notes: A varying load is a motor duty term; 422.13 sizing at 125 percent matches a continuous load.
Intermittent loads are not sized at 125 percent; 422.13 treats the water heater like a continuous load.
Noncontinuous loads are sized at 100 percent; 422.13 requires 125 percent for the water heater.
422.13 requires the overcurrent device and conductors to be rated at least 125 percent of the water heater rating, the continuous-load sizing.
open-book-exam-#11-014.tip_short: Storage water heaters of 120 gallons or less: size the breaker and wire at 125 percent of the heater rating, like any continuous load. Correct: D — continuous load. 422.13 requires the overcurrent device and conductors to be rated at least 125 percent of the water heater rating, the continuous-load sizing.

open-book-exam-#11-015.gist: Ground-fault protection on large services only works if its sensors and settings are right in the finished installation. The question asks when the system must be performance tested.
open-book-exam-#11-015.reference_text:
230.95(C) Performance Testing
The ground-fault protection system shall be performance tested when first installed on site. This testing shall be conducted by a qualified person(s) using a test process of primary current injection, in accordance with instructions that shall be provided with the equipment. A written record of this testing shall be made and shall be available to the authority having jurisdiction.
choice_notes: The AHJ does not perform the test; 230.95(C) requires a qualified person, with the record available to the AHJ.
Design review is not a test; 230.95(C) requires performance testing when first installed on site.
Factory testing does not satisfy 230.95(C); the system is tested when first installed on site.
230.95(C) requires the ground-fault protection system to be performance tested when first installed on site.
open-book-exam-#11-015.tip_short: Service GFPE must be performance tested when first installed on site, by a qualified person using primary current injection, with a written record. Correct: D — when first installed on site. Not A: The AHJ does not perform the test; 230.95(C) requires a qualified person, with the record available to the AHJ. Not B: Design review is not a test; 230.95(C) requires performance testing when first installed on site. Not C: Factory testing does not satisfy 230.95(C); the system is tested when first installed on site.

open-book-exam-#11-016.gist: Hallway and lobby lights must stay on no matter what one tenant does with their own panel. The question asks what kind of individual space the common-area circuits must not be fed from.
open-book-exam-#11-016.reference_text:
210.25(B) Common Area Branch Circuits
Branch circuits installed for lighting, central alarm, signal, communications, or other purposes for public or common areas of a two-family dwelling, a multifamily dwelling, or a multi-occupancy building shall not be supplied from equipment that supplies an individual dwelling unit or tenant space.
choice_notes: 210.25(B) prohibits common area branch circuits from equipment that supplies an individual dwelling unit or tenant space.
A branch circuit is not a space; 210.25(B) refers to an individual dwelling unit or tenant space.
The service supplies the whole building; 210.25(B) is about equipment for an individual dwelling unit.
A feeder is a set of conductors, not a space; 210.25(B) refers to an individual dwelling unit.
open-book-exam-#11-016.tip_short: Common-area circuits come from house equipment, never from a panel that supplies an individual dwelling unit or tenant space. Correct: A — dwelling unit.

open-book-exam-#11-017.prompt: Pendant conductors longer than 36 inches shall be twisted together where not cabled in a/an ___ assembly.
open-book-exam-#11-017.gist: Long pendant leads for a hanging lampholder can separate and chafe unless they are held together. The question asks what kind of cabled assembly avoids the twisting rule.
open-book-exam-#11-017.reference_text:
410.54(C) Twisted or Cabled
Pendant conductors longer than 900 mm (3 ft) shall be twisted together where not cabled in a listed assembly.
choice_notes: Approved is not the term in 410.54(C); the assembly must be listed.
410.54(C) requires twisting of pendant conductors longer than 900 mm (3 feet) where not cabled in a listed assembly.
Identified is not the term in 410.54(C); the assembly must be listed.
Suitable is not the term in 410.54(C); the assembly must be listed.
open-book-exam-#11-017.tip_short: Pendant conductors over 3 feet are twisted together unless cabled in a listed assembly. Correct: B — listed.

open-book-exam-#11-018.prompt: In other than one- and two-family dwelling units, the available fault current and the date the calculation was performed shall be field marked on the enclosure of ___.
open-book-exam-#11-018.gist: Workers and inspectors need to know how much fault current the gear could see, and when that number was figured. The question asks which distribution equipment gets the field marking.
open-book-exam-#11-018.reference_text:
408.6 Short-Circuit Current Rating
Switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards shall have a short-circuit current rating not less than the available fault current. In other than one- and two-family dwelling units, the available fault current and the date the calculation was performed shall be field marked on the enclosure at the point of supply. The marking shall comply with 110.21(B)(3).
choice_notes: Switchgear is included, but 408.6 also covers switchboards and panelboards.
Panelboards are included, but 408.6 also covers switchboards and switchgear.
Switchboards are included, but 408.6 also covers switchgear and panelboards.
408.6 applies to switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards, so all of these are field marked.
open-book-exam-#11-018.tip_short: Outside one- and two-family dwellings, switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards are field marked with the available fault current and the calculation date. Correct: D — all of these.

open-book-exam-#11-019.gist: Load calculations need a minimum value for an EV charger even when its nameplate is small. The question asks that minimum in volt-amperes.
open-book-exam-#11-019.reference_text:
220.57 Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment (EVSE) Load
The EVSE load shall be calculated at either 7200 watts (volt-amperes) or the nameplate rating of the equipment, whichever is larger.
choice_notes: 3,600 volt-amperes is too low; 220.57 uses 7200 volt-amperes or the nameplate.
5,000 volt-amperes is the dryer minimum in 220.54, not the EVSE value.
6,000 volt-amperes is not the EVSE value; 220.57 uses 7200 volt-amperes or the nameplate.
220.57 calculates the EVSE load at 7200 watts (volt-amperes) or the nameplate rating, whichever is larger.
open-book-exam-#11-019.tip_short: EVSE load in a calculation: 7200 volt-amperes or the nameplate rating, whichever is larger. Correct: D — 7,200. 220.57 calculates the EVSE load at 7200 watts (volt-amperes) or the nameplate rating, whichever is larger.

open-book-exam-#11-020.gist: A ground ring is bare copper buried around a building to serve as a grounding electrode, so it needs a minimum size to last in the earth. The question asks that minimum size.
open-book-exam-#11-020.reference_text:
250.52(A)(4) Ground Ring
A ground ring encircling the building or structure, in direct contact with the earth, consisting of at least 6.0 m (20 ft) of bare copper conductor not smaller than 2 AWG.
choice_notes: 8 AWG is too small; 250.52(A)(4) requires a ground ring of bare copper not smaller than 2 AWG.
6 AWG is too small; 250.52(A)(4) requires a ground ring not smaller than 2 AWG.
4 AWG is the bare copper size for a concrete-encased electrode, not a ground ring.
250.52(A)(4) requires a ground ring of at least 20 feet of bare copper not smaller than 2 AWG.
open-book-exam-#11-020.tip_short: Ground ring: at least 20 feet of bare copper not smaller than 2 AWG, encircling the building in contact with earth. Correct: D — #2. 250.52(A)(4) requires a ground ring of at least 20 feet of bare copper not smaller than 2 AWG. Not A: 8 AWG is too small; 250.52(A)(4) requires a ground ring of bare copper not smaller than 2 AWG. Not B: 6 AWG is too small; 250.52(A)(4) requires a ground ring not smaller than 2 AWG. Not C: 4 AWG is the bare copper size for a concrete-encased electrode, not a ground ring.

open-book-exam-#11-021.prompt: All nonlocking, 15 and 20 amp, 125-volt through 250-volt receptacles located in ___ must be listed as tamper-resistant.
open-book-exam-#11-021.gist: Children can push objects into receptacle slots, so the Code requires shuttered receptacles wherever families live. The question asks which of the listed locations are covered.
open-book-exam-#11-021.reference_text:
406.12 Tamper-Resistant Receptacles
All 15- and 20-ampere, 125- and 250-volt nonlocking-type receptacles in the following locations shall be listed tamper-resistant receptacles:
All dwelling units, boathouses, mobile homes and manufactured homes, including their attached and detached garages, accessory buildings, and common areas
choice_notes: Dwelling units are covered, but 406.12(1) also includes accessory buildings and common areas.
Accessory buildings are covered, but 406.12(1) also includes the dwelling units and common areas.
Common areas are covered, but 406.12(1) also includes dwelling units and accessory buildings.
406.12(1) requires listed tamper-resistant receptacles in dwelling units, their accessory buildings, and common areas.
open-book-exam-#11-021.tip_short: Tamper-resistant receptacles: all dwelling units plus their garages, accessory buildings, and common areas. Correct: D — all of these. 406.12(1) requires listed tamper-resistant receptacles in dwelling units, their accessory buildings, and common areas. Not B: Accessory buildings are covered, but 406.12(1) also includes the dwelling units and common areas. Not C: Common areas are covered, but 406.12(1) also includes dwelling units and accessory buildings.

open-book-exam-#11-022.gist: Sometimes putting a disconnect at the motor itself is impractical or more dangerous, so the Code lets the controller's disconnect do the job if it can be secured off. The question asks the condition.
open-book-exam-#11-022.reference_text:
430.102(B) Motor
A disconnecting means shall be provided for a motor in accordance with 430.102(B)(1) or (B)(2).
Exception to (1) and (2): The disconnecting means for the motor shall not be required under either of the following conditions if the motor controller disconnecting means required in 430.102(A) is lockable in accordance with 110.25:
(1) Where such a location of the disconnecting means for the motor is impracticable or introduces additional or increased hazards to persons or property
choice_notes: Serviceable is not the condition; the 430.102(B) exception requires the controller disconnect to be lockable.
Accessible is not the condition; the 430.102(B) exception requires the controller disconnect to be lockable per 110.25.
The 430.102(B) exception requires the motor controller disconnecting means to be lockable in accordance with 110.25.
Readily accessible is not the condition; the 430.102(B) exception requires lockable per 110.25.
open-book-exam-#11-022.tip_short: No motor disconnect is needed where it would add hazards, if the controller disconnect is lockable open per 110.25. Correct: C — lockable.
open-book-exam-#11-022.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: motor, disconnecting means. Start with 430.102(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#11-023.gist: Box fill counts each device on a yoke as if it were a number of conductors, no matter how many terminals it has. The question asks how many conductors a three-way switch counts as.
open-book-exam-#11-023.reference_text:
314.16(B)(4) Device or Equipment Fill
For each yoke or strap containing one or more devices or equipment, a double volume allowance in accordance with Table 314.16(B)(1) shall be made for each yoke or strap based on the largest conductor connected to a device(s) or equipment supported by that yoke or strap.
choice_notes: One is the allowance for clamps or support fittings; a device yoke gets a double allowance in 314.16(B)(4).
314.16(B)(4) requires a double volume allowance for each yoke or strap, based on the largest conductor connected.
Three is not the count; the number of terminals does not matter, each yoke gets a double allowance.
Devices must be counted; 314.16(B)(4) requires a double volume allowance for each yoke.
open-book-exam-#11-023.tip_short: Every device yoke counts as two conductors of the largest size connected to it, whether a single-pole, three-way, or duplex receptacle. Correct: B — two. 314.16(B)(4) requires a double volume allowance for each yoke or strap, based on the largest conductor connected. Not D: Devices must be counted; 314.16(B)(4) requires a double volume allowance for each yoke.

open-book-exam-#11-024.gist: Small dry-type transformers are sometimes tucked above drop ceilings, where they are not readily accessible. The question asks the largest kVA rating allowed in such a hollow space.
open-book-exam-#11-024.reference_text:
450.13(B) Hollow Space Installations
Dry-type transformers 1000 volts, nominal, or less and not exceeding 50 kVA shall be permitted in hollow spaces of buildings not permanently closed in by structure, provided they meet the ventilation requirements of 450.9 and separation from combustible materials requirements of 450.21(A). Transformers so installed shall not be required to be readily accessible.
choice_notes: 450.13(B) permits dry-type transformers 1000 volts or less and not exceeding 50 kVA in hollow spaces.
60 kVA exceeds the 50 kVA limit in 450.13(B) for hollow space installations.
75 kVA exceeds the 50 kVA limit in 450.13(B); 112 1/2 kVA is the threshold in 450.21 for fire-resistant rooms.
115 kVA far exceeds the 50 kVA limit in 450.13(B) for hollow space installations.
open-book-exam-#11-024.tip_short: Dry-type transformers up to 1000 volts and 50 kVA may go in hollow spaces like above a lay-in ceiling, with ventilation and clearance to combustibles. Correct: A — 50.

open-book-exam-#11-025.gist: Mineral-insulated cable is a rigid copper-sheathed cable, stiffer than most, so it needs less frequent support than NM or AC cable. The question asks the maximum support interval.
open-book-exam-#11-025.reference_text:
332.30 Securing and Supporting
Type MI cable shall be supported and secured by staples, straps, hangers, or similar fittings, designed and installed so as not to damage the cable, at intervals not exceeding 1.8 m (6 ft).
choice_notes: 3 feet is closer than required; 332.30 allows MI cable support at intervals up to 6 feet.
48 inches is closer than required; 332.30 allows up to 6 feet between supports.
5 feet is closer than required; 332.30 allows up to 6 feet between supports.
332.30 requires Type MI cable to be supported and secured at intervals not exceeding 1.8 m (6 feet).
open-book-exam-#11-025.tip_short: MI cable is supported and secured at intervals not exceeding 6 feet. Correct: D — 6 feet. Not B: 48 inches is closer than required; 332.30 allows up to 6 feet between supports.

open-book-exam-#12-001.prompt: If an exit enclosure (stair tower) is required to have a fire resistance rating, only electrical wiring methods serving equipment permitted by the ___ shall be installed within the exit enclosure.
open-book-exam-#12-001.gist: A fire-rated stair tower is the escape route during a fire, so the Code keeps unrelated wiring out of it. The question asks who decides which equipment may have wiring inside it.
open-book-exam-#12-001.reference_text:
300.25 Exit Enclosures (Stair Towers)
Where an exit enclosure is required to have a fire resistance rating, only electrical wiring methods serving equipment permitted by the authority having jurisdiction in the exit enclosure shall be installed within the exit enclosure.
choice_notes: The electrical inspector may act for the authority, but 300.25 names the authority having jurisdiction.
A building inspector is not the term used; 300.25 leaves the decision to the authority having jurisdiction.
The fire marshal may be the AHJ in some places, but 300.25 names the authority having jurisdiction.
300.25 allows only wiring methods serving equipment permitted by the authority having jurisdiction in the exit enclosure.
open-book-exam-#12-001.tip_short: Fire-rated exit stair towers carry only wiring for equipment the authority having jurisdiction permits there (300.25). Correct: D — AHJ. 300.25 allows only wiring methods serving equipment permitted by the authority having jurisdiction in the exit enclosure.

open-book-exam-#12-002.gist: Large-scale PV plants are engineered supply stations run by qualified staff, not buildings people live or work in. The question asks how the rapid shutdown rule of 690.12 applies to buildings that only house that equipment.
open-book-exam-#12-002.reference_text:
691.9 Disconnecting Means for Isolating Photovoltaic Equipment
Buildings whose sole purpose is to house and protect supply station equipment shall not be required to comply with 690.12. Written standard operating procedures shall be available at the site detailing necessary shutdown procedures in the event of an emergency.
choice_notes: Never is not the Code wording; 691.9 says such buildings shall not be required to comply with 690.12.
691.9 exempts these buildings; they are not required to comply with 690.12.
691.9 says buildings whose sole purpose is to house and protect supply station equipment shall not be required to comply with 690.12.
Always is the opposite of 691.9, which exempts these buildings from 690.12.
open-book-exam-#12-002.tip_short: Large-scale PV (Article 691): buildings that only house supply station equipment are exempt from 690.12 rapid shutdown, but written shutdown procedures must be on site. Correct: C — not be required to. Not B: 691.9 exempts these buildings; they are not required to comply with 690.12.

open-book-exam-#12-003.gist: At a fuel dispenser, even a current-carrying conductor that is near ground potential can spark in the vapor area. The question asks which conductor the emergency shutoff must also open.
open-book-exam-#12-003.reference_text:
514.11(A) Emergency Electrical Disconnects
The emergency shutoff device shall disconnect simultaneously from the source of supply, all conductors of the circuits, including the grounded conductor, if any. Equipment grounding conductors shall remain connected.
choice_notes: 514.11(A) requires the emergency shutoff to disconnect all circuit conductors, including the grounded conductor.
A grounding electrode conductor is not a circuit conductor at the dispenser and is never opened by the shutoff.
514.11(A) says equipment grounding conductors shall remain connected.
Not all of these; equipment grounding conductors must remain connected under 514.11(A).
open-book-exam-#12-003.tip_short: Fuel dispenser emergency shutoff (514.11(A)): open every circuit conductor at once, including the grounded conductor; the equipment grounding conductor stays connected. Correct: A — grounded.

open-book-exam-#12-004.gist: Life-safety circuits must keep working when a fault or fire damages ordinary wiring nearby. The question asks which kind of loads must have wiring kept entirely separate.
open-book-exam-#12-004.reference_text:
700.10(B) Wiring
Wiring from an emergency source or emergency source distribution overcurrent protection to emergency loads shall be kept entirely independent of all other wiring and equipment unless otherwise permitted in the following:
choice_notes: 700.10(B) requires wiring to emergency loads to be kept entirely independent of all other wiring and equipment.
Legally required standby wiring may occupy the same raceways, cables, boxes, and cabinets with other general wiring (701.10).
Optional standby wiring has no independence requirement; it may be run with general wiring (702.10).
Not all of these; only emergency system wiring must be kept independent (700.10(B)).
open-book-exam-#12-004.tip_short: Emergency system wiring (700.10(B)) is kept entirely independent of all other wiring; legally required and optional standby wiring may share raceways with general wiring. Correct: A — emergency. Not B: Legally required standby wiring may occupy the same raceways, cables, boxes, and cabinets with other general wiring (701.10).

open-book-exam-#12-005.gist: A building normally gets one service, but very large loads can outgrow what one service can carry. The question asks the capacity above which extra services are allowed.
open-book-exam-#12-005.reference_text:
230.2(C) Capacity Requirements
Additional services shall be permitted under any of the following:
(1) Where the capacity requirements are in excess of 2000 amperes at a supply voltage of 1000 volts or less
choice_notes: 1000 amperes is below the 230.2(C)(1) threshold of 2000 amperes.
1200 amperes is below the 230.2(C)(1) threshold of 2000 amperes.
230.2(C)(1) permits additional services where capacity requirements exceed 2000 amperes at 1000 volts or less.
2400 amperes is above the threshold; additional services are already permitted over 2000 amperes.
open-book-exam-#12-005.tip_short: Additional services (230.2(C)(1)): capacity over 2000 amperes at 1000 volts or less. Correct: C — 2,000. 230.2(C)(1) permits additional services where capacity requirements exceed 2000 amperes at 1000 volts or less. Not A: 1000 amperes is below the 230.2(C)(1) threshold of 2000 amperes. Not B: 1200 amperes is below the 230.2(C)(1) threshold of 2000 amperes. Not D: 2400 amperes is above the threshold; additional services are already permitted over 2000 amperes.
open-book-exam-#12-005.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 230.2(C), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#12-006.prompt: Equipment intended to interrupt current at fault levels shall have a/an ___ rating, at nominal circuit voltage, that is at least equal to the available fault current at the line terminals of the equipment.
open-book-exam-#12-006.gist: A breaker or fuse that opens a fault larger than it was built for can explode. The question asks which rating must be at least the available fault current.
open-book-exam-#12-006.reference_text:
110.9 Interrupting Rating
Equipment intended to interrupt current at fault levels shall have an interrupting rating at nominal circuit voltage at least equal to the available fault current at the line terminals of the equipment.
choice_notes: A time delay describes how fast a device trips, not how much fault current it can safely open.
110.9 requires an interrupting rating at nominal circuit voltage at least equal to the available fault current.
A short-time rating is a breaker trip setting or withstand, not the 110.9 interrupting rating.
A long-time setting is the overload pickup of a breaker, not the 110.9 interrupting rating.
open-book-exam-#12-006.tip_short: Breakers and fuses need an interrupting rating at least equal to the available fault current at their line terminals (110.9). Correct: B — interrupting.

open-book-exam-#12-007.gist: A microgrid can run connected to the utility or cut loose and supply its own loads. The question asks the Code's name for running on its own.
open-book-exam-#12-007.reference_text:
705.50 System Operation
Interconnected microgrid systems shall be capable of operating in interactive mode with a primary source of power, or electric utility, or other electric power production and distribution network. Microgrid systems shall be permitted to disconnect from other sources and operate in island mode.
choice_notes: Standby describes a backup source, not the 705.50 operating mode of a disconnected microgrid.
Stand-alone describes a system never connected to other sources; 705.50 calls this island mode.
Parallel (interactive) operation is the connected mode, the opposite of disconnecting.
705.50 permits microgrid systems to disconnect from other sources and operate in island mode.
open-book-exam-#12-007.tip_short: Microgrids (705.50) run interactive with the utility or disconnect and operate in island mode. Correct: D — island mode. Not A: Standby describes a backup source, not the 705.50 operating mode of a disconnected microgrid. Not B: Stand-alone describes a system never connected to other sources; 705.50 calls this island mode.

open-book-exam-#12-008.gist: A hole cut for a raceway can let fire and smoke pass through a rated assembly. The question asks which rated assemblies need their penetrations firestopped.
open-book-exam-#12-008.reference_text:
300.21 Spread of Fire or Products of Combustion
Electrical installations in hollow spaces, vertical shafts, and ventilation or air-handling ducts shall be made so that the possible spread of fire or products of combustion will not be substantially increased. Openings around electrical penetrations into or through fire-resistant-rated walls, partitions, floors, or ceilings shall be firestopped using approved methods to maintain the fire resistance rating.
choice_notes: Walls are included, but 300.21 also names partitions, floors, and ceilings.
Floors are included, but 300.21 also names walls, partitions, and ceilings.
Ceilings are included, but 300.21 also names walls, partitions, and floors.
300.21 requires firestopping of penetrations through fire-resistant-rated walls, partitions, floors, or ceilings.
open-book-exam-#12-008.tip_short: Firestop every penetration through a fire-rated wall, partition, floor, or ceiling to keep its rating (300.21). Correct: D — all of these. 300.21 requires firestopping of penetrations through fire-resistant-rated walls, partitions, floors, or ceilings.

open-book-exam-#12-009.gist: PV dc circuits can stay energized whenever the sun shines, so they are kept apart from the ac side. The question asks where they may not share space with the ac conductors.
open-book-exam-#12-009.reference_text:
690.31(B)(1) Conductors of Different Systems
Where not otherwise allowed in an equipment's listing, PV system dc circuits shall not occupy the same equipment wiring enclosure, cable, or raceway as other non-PV systems or inverter output circuits unless separated from other circuits by a barrier or partition.
choice_notes: A raceway is included, but 690.31(B)(1) also names the equipment wiring enclosure and cable.
A cable is included, but 690.31(B)(1) also names the equipment wiring enclosure and raceway.
An enclosure is included, but 690.31(B)(1) also names the cable and raceway.
690.31(B)(1) keeps PV dc circuits out of the same enclosure, cable, or raceway as inverter output circuits unless separated by a barrier.
open-book-exam-#12-009.tip_short: PV dc circuits stay out of the same enclosure, cable, or raceway as inverter output (ac) circuits unless a barrier separates them (690.31(B)(1)). Correct: D — all of these. 690.31(B)(1) keeps PV dc circuits out of the same enclosure, cable, or raceway as inverter output circuits unless separated by a barrier.

open-book-exam-#12-010.gist: On a center-tapped delta, one phase sits much higher above ground than the other two, and connecting a 120-volt load to it causes damage. The question asks how else that conductor may be marked besides its standard color.
open-book-exam-#12-010.reference_text:
110.15 High-Leg Marking
On a 4-wire, delta-connected system where the midpoint of one phase winding is grounded, only the conductor or busbar having the higher phase voltage to ground shall be durably and permanently marked by an outer finish that is orange in color or by other effective means. Such identification shall be placed at each point on the system where a connection is made if the grounded conductor is also present.
choice_notes: Gray identifies a grounded conductor (200.6), so it cannot mark the high leg.
Yellow is not named in 110.15; the high leg is orange or marked by other effective means.
Brown is a common phase color by custom, not the 110.15 alternative marking.
110.15 requires an orange outer finish or other effective means on the high leg.
open-book-exam-#12-010.tip_short: High leg (110.15): mark it orange or by other effective means at every point where the grounded conductor is also present. Correct: D — other effective means.

open-book-exam-#12-011.gist: A fire pump motor must deliver full pressure during a fire, and low voltage cuts its torque. The question asks the voltage drop limit while the motor runs at 115 percent of full-load current.
open-book-exam-#12-011.reference_text:
695.7(D) Motor Running
The voltage at the contactor load terminals to which the motor is connected shall not drop more than 5 percent below the voltage rating of the motor when the motor is operating at 115 percent of the full-load current rating of the motor. [20:9.4.4]
choice_notes: 1.2 percent is not a 695.7 limit; the running limit at the load terminals is 5 percent.
3 percent is the common branch-circuit voltage drop recommendation, not the 695.7(D) limit.
695.7(D) limits the running voltage drop at the contactor load terminals to 5 percent at 115 percent of full-load current.
7.5 percent is more than 695.7(D) allows; the running limit is 5 percent.
open-book-exam-#12-011.tip_short: Fire pump voltage drop (695.7): 15 percent at the controller line terminals while starting, 5 percent at the motor terminals while running at 115 percent of full-load current. Correct: C — 5.

open-book-exam-#12-012.gist: Trees sway, grow, and fall in storms, which strains anything tied to them. The question asks what the Code forbids hanging on a tree.
open-book-exam-#12-012.reference_text:
225.26 Vegetation as Support
Vegetation such as trees shall not be used for support of overhead conductor spans.
410.36(G) Trees
Outdoor luminaires and associated equipment shall be permitted to be supported by trees.
choice_notes: 410.36(G) permits outdoor luminaires and associated equipment to be supported by trees.
Boxes for an outdoor luminaire are associated equipment that 410.36(G) permits on trees.
225.26 says vegetation such as trees shall not be used for support of overhead conductor spans.
Not any of these; luminaires and associated equipment may be supported by trees (410.36(G)).
open-book-exam-#12-012.tip_short: Trees may carry outdoor luminaires and their equipment (410.36(G)), but never overhead conductor spans (225.26). Correct: C — overhead conductor spans.

open-book-exam-#12-013.prompt: A/an ___ listed shall be installed between a wind electric system and any loads served by the premises electrical system.
open-book-exam-#12-013.gist: A wind turbine on a tall tower is a lightning target, and the surges travel down into the building wiring. The question asks which listed device goes between the wind system and the premises loads.
open-book-exam-#12-013.reference_text:
694.7(D) Overvoltage Protection
A listed surge protective device shall be installed between a wind electric system and any loads served by the premises electrical system. The SPD shall be permitted to be a Type 3 SPD on the circuit serving a wind electric system or a Type 2 SPD located anywhere on the load side of the service disconnect. SPDs shall be installed in accordance with Part II of Article 242.
choice_notes: 694.7(D) requires a listed surge protective device between a wind electric system and premises loads.
A GFCI protects people from ground faults; it does not limit lightning surges from the wind system.
An AFCI detects arcing faults in branch circuits; it does not provide the overvoltage protection 694.7(D) requires.
A surge arrester is used over 1000 volts; 694.7(D) calls for a listed surge protective device (SPD).
open-book-exam-#12-013.tip_short: Wind electric systems (694.7(D)) need a listed SPD between the system and premises loads: Type 3 on the wind circuit or Type 2 on the load side of the service disconnect. Correct: A — surge protective device.

open-book-exam-#12-014.gist: A light inside a commercial kitchen hood sits in the airstream pulled off the cooking surface. The question asks what else, besides grease and oil, must be kept out of its lamp and wiring compartment.
open-book-exam-#12-014.reference_text:
410.10(C) In Ducts or Hoods
Luminaires shall be permitted to be installed in commercial cooking hoods where all of the following conditions are met:
(2) The luminaire shall be constructed so that all exhaust vapors, grease, oil, or cooking vapors are excluded from the lamp and wiring compartment. Diffusers shall be resistant to thermal shock.
choice_notes: Solids are not named in 410.10(C)(2); the luminaire must exclude exhaust vapors, grease, oil, and cooking vapors.
Moisture is not in the 410.10(C)(2) list; it names exhaust vapors, grease, oil, and cooking vapors.
Oxygen cannot practically be excluded and is not in the 410.10(C)(2) list.
410.10(C)(2) requires all exhaust vapors, grease, oil, or cooking vapors to be excluded from the lamp and wiring compartment.
open-book-exam-#12-014.tip_short: Hood luminaires (410.10(C)): identified for the use, sealed against exhaust vapors, grease, oil, and cooking vapors, corrosion resistant and smooth, with no wiring exposed in the hood. Correct: D — exhaust vapors.
open-book-exam-#12-014.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 410.10(C), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#12-015.gist: Inverters, dc-to-dc converters, and charge controllers all change power from one form to another. The question asks the general Code term that covers every such device.
open-book-exam-#12-015.reference_text:
Article 100 Definitions — Electronic Power Converter
Electronic Power Converter. A device that uses power electronics to convert one form of electrical power into another form of electrical power. (CMP—4)
Informational Note: Examples of electronic power converters include, but are not limited to, inverters, dc-to-dc converters, and electronic charge controllers.
choice_notes: A solar cell converts light into electricity; it does not convert one form of electrical power into another.
A wind turbine converts wind energy into electricity; it is not the Article 100 term for a power converter.
An inverter is one example of an electronic power converter, but it only changes dc to ac.
Article 100 defines an electronic power converter as a device that uses power electronics to convert one form of electrical power into another.
open-book-exam-#12-015.tip_short: Electronic power converter (Article 100) is the umbrella term; inverters, dc-to-dc converters, and charge controllers are examples. Correct: D — electronic power converter.

open-book-exam-#12-016.gist: Two different metals touching in a wet or chemical setting can corrode each other through galvanic action. The question asks the condition under which stainless RMC may still be used with galvanized boxes.
open-book-exam-#12-016.reference_text:
344.14 Dissimilar Metals
Where practicable, dissimilar metals in contact anywhere in the system shall be avoided to eliminate the possibility of galvanic action. Stainless steel and aluminum fittings and enclosures shall be permitted to be used with galvanized steel RMC, and galvanized steel fittings and enclosures shall be permitted to be used with aluminum RMC where not subject to severe corrosive influences. Stainless steel rigid conduit shall only be used with the following:
(1) Stainless steel fittings
(2) Stainless steel boxes and enclosures
(3) Steel (galvanized, painted, powder or PVC coated, and so forth) boxes and enclosures when not subject to severe corrosive influences
(4) Stainless steel, nonmetallic, or approved accessories
choice_notes: 344.14(3) permits galvanized steel boxes and enclosures with stainless steel RMC when not subject to severe corrosive influences.
Unauthorized contact is a guarding concern, not the dissimilar metals limit of 344.14.
344.14 limits the mix only where influences are severe, not where there are any corrosive influences at all.
Physical damage is a separate protection concern; 344.14 is about corrosion from dissimilar metals.
open-book-exam-#12-016.tip_short: Stainless RMC (344.14) mixes with galvanized or coated steel boxes only where there are no severe corrosive influences. Correct: A — severe corrosive influences.

open-book-exam-#12-017.prompt: For a PV system, the rapid shutdown for conductors outside the array boundary must limit the voltage to not more than ___ volts within 30 seconds of the shutdown initiation.
open-book-exam-#12-017.gist: Firefighters on a roof or in an attic need PV circuits brought down to a safe voltage quickly after shutdown. The question asks the voltage limit for the controlled conductors beyond the array.
open-book-exam-#12-017.reference_text:
690.12(B)(1) Outside the Array Boundary
Controlled conductors located outside the boundary or more than 1 m (3 ft) from the point of entry inside a building shall be limited to not more than 30 volts within 30 seconds of rapid shutdown initiation. Voltage shall be measured between any two conductors and between any conductor and ground.
choice_notes: 10 volts is not a 690.12(B) limit; outside the array boundary the limit is 30 volts.
15 volts is not a 690.12(B) limit; outside the array boundary the limit is 30 volts.
24 volts is not a 690.12(B) limit; outside the array boundary the limit is 30 volts.
690.12(B)(1) limits controlled conductors outside the array boundary to 30 volts within 30 seconds of rapid shutdown initiation.
open-book-exam-#12-017.tip_short: PV rapid shutdown (690.12(B)): outside the array boundary, 30 volts within 30 seconds; inside it, a listed hazard control system or 80 volts within 30 seconds. Correct: D — 30.

open-book-exam-#12-018.gist: When one cable tray carries both multiconductor and single-conductor cables, each kind uses up part of the tray's allowable fill. The question asks the limit on the two shares added together.
open-book-exam-#12-018.reference_text:
392.80(A)(3) Combinations of Multiconductor and Single-Conductor Cables
Where a cable tray contains a combination of multiconductor and single-conductor cables, the ampacities shall be as given in 392.80(A)(1) for multiconductor cables and 392.80(A)(2) for single-conductor cables, provided that the following conditions apply:
The sum of the multiconductor cable fill area as a percentage of the allowable fill area for the tray calculated in accordance with 392.22(A), and the single-conductor cable fill area as a percentage of the allowable fill area for the tray calculated in accordance with 392.22(B), totals not more than 100 percent.
choice_notes: 75 percent is a single-conductor ampacity factor in 392.80(A)(2), not the combined fill limit.
80 percent is not the 392.80(A)(3) limit; the two fill percentages may total 100 percent.
392.80(A)(3) permits the two fill percentages to total not more than 100 percent.
125 percent would overfill the tray; 392.80(A)(3) caps the total at 100 percent.
open-book-exam-#12-018.tip_short: Mixed cable tray (392.80(A)(3)): the multiconductor share plus the single-conductor share of allowable fill may not exceed 100 percent. Correct: C — 100.

open-book-exam-#12-019.gist: A battery energy storage system both charges and discharges, so it has a voltage rating each way. The question asks which rated voltage, along with the input, sets its maximum voltage.
open-book-exam-#12-019.reference_text:
706.9 Maximum Voltage
The maximum voltage of an ESS shall be the rated ESS input and output voltage(s) indicated on the ESS nameplate(s) or system listing.
choice_notes: 706.9 sets the maximum voltage as the rated ESS input and output voltage(s) on the nameplate or listing.
Line voltage is not the 706.9 term; the rule uses the rated input and output voltages.
Secondary voltage describes a transformer winding, not the 706.9 ESS rating.
Load voltage is not the 706.9 term; the rule uses the rated input and output voltages.
open-book-exam-#12-019.tip_short: ESS maximum voltage (706.9) is the rated input and output voltage(s) on the nameplate or system listing. Correct: A — output.

open-book-exam-#12-020.gist: Some tray cable carries only tiny instrument signals and is not meant for power. The question asks which kind of wire in Type TC cable must not carry a voltage marking.
open-book-exam-#12-020.reference_text:
336.120 Marking
There shall be no voltage marking on a Type TC cable employing thermocouple extension wire.
choice_notes: Covered wire is not the 336.120 exception; the rule names thermocouple extension wire.
Fixture wire is not the 336.120 exception; the rule names thermocouple extension wire.
Rubber insulated wire is not the 336.120 exception; the rule names thermocouple extension wire.
336.120 prohibits a voltage marking on Type TC cable employing thermocouple extension wire.
open-book-exam-#12-020.tip_short: Type TC with thermocouple extension wire gets no voltage marking (336.120), so no one mistakes it for power cable. Correct: D — thermocouple extension.

open-book-exam-#12-021.gist: Flexible metallic tubing is a light, liquidtight tubing meant for short runs in dry, accessible places. The question asks the largest trade size made for it.
open-book-exam-#12-021.reference_text:
360.20(B) Maximum
The maximum size of FMT shall be metric designator 21 (trade size 3/4).
choice_notes: Trade size 1/2 is the minimum size of FMT in 360.20(A), not the maximum.
360.20(B) limits FMT to metric designator 21, trade size 3/4.
Trade size 1 is larger than the 360.20(B) maximum of trade size 3/4.
Trade size 1 1/4 is larger than the 360.20(B) maximum of trade size 3/4.
open-book-exam-#12-021.tip_short: FMT (360.20): trade size 1/2 minimum (3/8 in some uses), trade size 3/4 maximum. Correct: B — 3/4". 360.20(B) limits FMT to metric designator 21, trade size 3/4. Not A: Trade size 1/2 is the minimum size of FMT in 360.20(A), not the maximum. Not C: Trade size 1 is larger than the 360.20(B) maximum of trade size 3/4. Not D: Trade size 1 1/4 is larger than the 360.20(B) maximum of trade size 3/4.

open-book-exam-#12-022.gist: EMT normally has to be strapped close to every box it enters, but framing does not always line up. The question asks how far the first strap may move on an unbroken length when it cannot be within 3 feet.
open-book-exam-#12-022.reference_text:
358.30(A) Securely Fastened
EMT shall be securely fastened in place in accordance with the following:
(1) At intervals not to exceed 3 m (10 ft)
(2) Within 900 mm (3 ft) of each outlet box, junction box, device box, cabinet, conduit body, or other tubing termination
Exception No. 1: Fastening of unbroken lengths shall be permitted to be increased to a distance of 1.5 m (5 ft) where structural members do not readily permit fastening within 900 mm (3 ft).
choice_notes: 4 feet is not the 358.30(A) Exception No. 1 distance; it allows up to 5 feet.
358.30(A) Exception No. 1 permits increasing the distance to 1.5 m (5 feet) on unbroken lengths.
6 feet is more than the 5 feet 358.30(A) Exception No. 1 allows.
10 feet is the spacing between supports along the run, not the distance from a termination.
open-book-exam-#12-022.tip_short: EMT support (358.30(A)): every 10 feet and within 3 feet of terminations, stretched to 5 feet on unbroken lengths where framing does not allow 3 feet. Correct: B — 5'. 358.30(A) Exception No. 1 permits increasing the distance to 1.5 m (5 feet) on unbroken lengths. Not A: 4 feet is not the 358.30(A) Exception No. 1 distance; it allows up to 5 feet. Not C: 6 feet is more than the 5 feet 358.30(A) Exception No. 1 allows. Not D: 10 feet is the spacing between supports along the run, not the distance from a termination.
open-book-exam-#12-022.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: conduit. Start with 358.30(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#12-023.gist: Motor branch circuits often have a breaker much larger than the wire, because motors draw a big starting current. The question asks how that affects the equipment grounding conductor size.
open-book-exam-#12-023.reference_text:
250.122(A) General
Copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum equipment grounding conductors of the wire type shall not be smaller than shown in Table 250.122. The equipment grounding conductor shall not be required to be larger than the circuit conductors supplying the equipment.
250.122(D)(1) General
The equipment grounding conductor size shall not be smaller than determined by 250.122(A) based on the rating of the branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protective device.
reference_table: NOTE: The EGC is not required to be larger than the circuit conductors supplying the equipment (250.122(A)).
choice_notes: Table 250.122 gives 10 AWG for 30 amperes, but 250.122(A) does not require the EGC to be larger than the 12 AWG circuit conductors.
8 AWG is the Table 250.122 size for a 100-ampere device and is larger than the circuit conductors.
250.122(A) caps the EGC at the size of the circuit conductors, so 12 AWG copper is enough here.
14 AWG is smaller than both the Table 250.122 size and the circuit conductors, so it is too small.
open-book-exam-#12-023.tip_short: Size the EGC from Table 250.122 by the overcurrent device, but it never has to be larger than the circuit conductors (250.122(A)). Correct: C — #12. 250.122(A) caps the EGC at the size of the circuit conductors, so 12 AWG copper is enough here. Not A: Table 250.122 gives 10 AWG for 30 amperes, but 250.122(A) does not require the EGC to be larger than the 12 AWG circuit conductors. Not B: 8 AWG is the Table 250.122 size for a 100-ampere device and is larger than the circuit conductors. Not D: 14 AWG is smaller than both the Table 250.122 size and the circuit conductors, so it is too small.
open-book-exam-#12-023.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: equipment grounding conductor, branch circuit, motor. Start with 250.122(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#12-024.prompt: In a high bay manufacturing building, what is the maximum total length of a feeder tap conductor permitted by the feeder tap rules?
open-book-exam-#12-024.gist: Feeder taps have no overcurrent device where they connect, so the Code limits how far they may run. The question asks the longest total length the tap rules allow in a tall manufacturing building.
open-book-exam-#12-024.reference_text:
240.21(B)(4) Taps Over 7.5 m (25 ft) Long
Where the feeder is in a high bay manufacturing building over 11 m (35 ft) high at walls and the installation complies with all the following conditions:
(2) The tap conductors are not over 7.5 m (25 ft) long horizontally and not over 30 m (100 ft) total length.
choice_notes: 10 feet is the 240.21(B)(1) tap rule, not the longest tap permitted in a high bay building.
25 feet is the 240.21(B)(2) tap rule and the horizontal limit in (B)(4), not the total length.
50 feet is not a 240.21(B) tap length.
240.21(B)(4)(2) allows taps not over 25 feet horizontally and not over 100 feet total in high bay manufacturing buildings.
open-book-exam-#12-024.tip_short: Feeder taps (240.21(B)): 10 feet, 25 feet, and in high bay manufacturing buildings up to 25 feet horizontal and 100 feet total; outside taps (B)(5) have no length limit. Correct: D — 100 feet.

open-book-exam-#12-025.gist: Overhead outside wiring must be high enough that people walking under it cannot touch it. The question asks the lowest clearance allowed above grade.
open-book-exam-#12-025.reference_text:
225.18 Clearance for Overhead Conductors and Cables
Overhead spans of open conductors and open multiconductor cables of not over 1000 volts, nominal, shall have a clearance of not less than the following:
(1) 3.0 m (10 ft) - above finished grade, sidewalks, or from any platform or projection that will permit personal contact where the voltage does not exceed 150 volts to ground and accessible to pedestrians only
choice_notes: 8 feet is less than the lowest 225.18 clearance of 10 feet.
225.18(1) requires 3.0 m (10 feet) above finished grade where the voltage does not exceed 150 volts to ground and only pedestrians have access.
15 feet is the 225.18(3) clearance for residential and commercial areas over 300 volts to ground.
18 feet is the 225.18(4) clearance over public streets, alleys, roads, and similar areas.
open-book-exam-#12-025.tip_short: Overhead clearances (225.18): 10, 12, 15, 18, and 24 1/2 feet; the lowest, 10 feet, is for 150 volts to ground or less over areas accessible to pedestrians only. Correct: B — 10.
open-book-exam-#12-025.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: cable, conductors. Start with 225.18, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#2-001.gist: A panelboard mounted flat collects dust, debris, and dropped tools on its live parts and is awkward to work on. The question asks which mounting position the Code forbids.
open-book-exam-#2-001.reference_text:
408.43 Panelboard Orientation
Panelboards shall not be installed in the face-up or face-down position.
choice_notes: 408.43 says panelboards shall not be installed in the face-up or face-down position.
Prone is not a Code term; 408.43 prohibits the face-up and face-down positions.
Posterior is not a Code term; 408.43 names the face-up and face-down positions.
Transverse is not a Code term; 408.43 only prohibits face-up or face-down mounting.
open-book-exam-#2-001.tip_short: Panelboards are never mounted lying flat: 408.43 forbids the face-up and face-down positions. Correct: A — face-up.

open-book-exam-#2-002.gist: A split-wired receptacle or a device fed by two circuits can stay live after one breaker is shut off. The question asks where the common disconnect for all of those circuits must be located.
open-book-exam-#2-002.reference_text:
210.7 Multiple Branch Circuits
If two or more branch circuits supply devices or equipment on the same yoke or mounting strap, a means to simultaneously disconnect the ungrounded supply conductors shall be provided at the point at which the branch circuits originate.
choice_notes: Starts is close in meaning, but 210.7 uses the word originate for the point where the disconnect goes.
The circuit terminates at the device itself; 210.7 requires the disconnect where the circuits originate.
210.7 requires the simultaneous disconnect at the point at which the branch circuits originate, usually the panelboard.
Separates is not the 210.7 wording; the disconnect is required where the branch circuits originate.
open-book-exam-#2-002.tip_short: Two circuits on one yoke need a simultaneous disconnect, such as a handle-tied breaker, where the circuits originate. Correct: C — originates. 210.7 requires the simultaneous disconnect at the point at which the branch circuits originate, usually the panelboard.

open-book-exam-#2-003.gist: A 15- or 20-ampere circuit that also feeds lights or plug-in loads needs room left for them, so fixed equipment on it is capped. The question asks what share of the circuit rating that fixed equipment may use.
open-book-exam-#2-003.reference_text:
210.23(B)(2) Utilization Equipment Fastened in Place
The total rating of utilization equipment fastened in place, other than luminaires, shall not exceed 50 percent of the branch-circuit ampere rating where lighting units, cord-and-plug-connected utilization equipment not fastened in place, or both, are also supplied.
choice_notes: 100 percent would leave nothing for the other loads; 210.23(B)(2) limits fixed equipment to 50 percent.
80 percent is the 210.23(B)(1) limit for one cord-and-plug item not fastened in place, not for fixed equipment.
75 percent is not a 210.23 limit; fastened-in-place equipment on a shared circuit is held to 50 percent.
210.23(B)(2) limits fastened-in-place equipment to 50 percent of the rating when lights or plug-in loads are also supplied.
open-book-exam-#2-003.tip_short: On a shared 15- or 20-ampere circuit, fastened-in-place equipment may total no more than half the circuit rating. Correct: D — 50%. 210.23(B)(2) limits fastened-in-place equipment to 50 percent of the rating when lights or plug-in loads are also supplied. Not A: 100 percent would leave nothing for the other loads; 210.23(B)(2) limits fixed equipment to 50 percent. Not B: 80 percent is the 210.23(B)(1) limit for one cord-and-plug item not fastened in place, not for fixed equipment. Not C: 75 percent is not a 210.23 limit; fastened-in-place equipment on a shared circuit is held to 50 percent.

open-book-exam-#2-004.gist: Crawl spaces are damp and put people close to the earth, so lighting outlets there need ground-fault protection up to a set voltage. The question asks that voltage.
choice_notes: 60 volts is not the 210.8(C) threshold; the rule covers crawl space lighting outlets up to 120 volts.
210.8(C) requires GFCI protection for crawl space lighting outlets not exceeding 120 volts.
240 volts is above the 210.8(C) limit; the rule covers lighting outlets not exceeding 120 volts.
300 volts is not used in 210.8(C); the rule covers lighting outlets not exceeding 120 volts.
open-book-exam-#2-004.tip_short: Crawl space lighting outlets up to 120 volts need GFCI protection because crawl spaces are damp and cramped. Correct: B — 120.

open-book-exam-#2-005.gist: Branch circuits that serve more than one outlet are designated by a fixed set of overcurrent device ratings. The question asks which list is that set.
open-book-exam-#2-005.reference_text:
210.18 Rating
Branch circuits recognized by this article shall be rated in accordance with the maximum permitted ampere rating or setting of the overcurrent device. The rating for other than individual branch circuits shall be 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amperes. Where conductors of higher ampacity are used for any reason, the ampere rating or setting of the specified overcurrent device shall determine the circuit rating.
choice_notes: 25 and 35 amperes are not branch circuit ratings under 210.18, and 10 and 15 amperes are missing.
25 amperes is not a 210.18 rating, and the 10 and 15 ampere ratings are missing.
25 amperes is not a 210.18 rating, and the 10 and 20 ampere ratings are missing.
210.18 lists 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amperes for other than individual branch circuits.
open-book-exam-#2-005.tip_short: Multioutlet branch circuit ratings are 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amperes. There is no 25 or 35. Correct: D — 10, 15, 20, 30, 40 and 50 amperes. 210.18 lists 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amperes for other than individual branch circuits. Not A: 25 and 35 amperes are not branch circuit ratings under 210.18, and 10 and 15 amperes are missing. Not B: 25 amperes is not a 210.18 rating, and the 10 and 15 ampere ratings are missing. Not C: 25 amperes is not a 210.18 rating, and the 10 and 20 ampere ratings are missing.

open-book-exam-#2-006.gist: Arc flash labels are aimed at the people who open energized equipment to work on it. The question asks which group of persons the marking is meant to warn.
open-book-exam-#2-006.reference_text:
110.16(A) General
Electrical equipment, such as switchboards, switchgear, enclosed panelboards, industrial control panels, meter socket enclosures, and motor control centers, that is in other than dwelling units, and is likely to require examination, adjustment, servicing, or maintenance while energized, shall be field or factory marked to warn qualified persons of potential electric arc flash hazards. The marking shall meet the requirements in 110.21(B) and shall be located so as to be clearly visible to qualified persons before examination, adjustment, servicing, or maintenance of the equipment.
choice_notes: The marking is not addressed to all persons; 110.16(A) says it warns qualified persons.
Maintenance is not the 110.16(A) term; the marking warns qualified persons.
110.16(A) requires the arc flash marking to warn qualified persons and to be visible to them before work.
Repairmen is not a Code term; 110.16(A) says the marking warns qualified persons.
open-book-exam-#2-006.tip_short: Arc flash warning labels on commercial and industrial gear are written for qualified persons who work on it energized. Correct: C — qualified.
open-book-exam-#2-006.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: dwelling unit. Start with 110.16(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#2-007.gist: Kitchen countertop appliances have short cords, so countertop receptacles along a wall must be close together. The question asks the farthest any point on the wall line may be from a receptacle.
open-book-exam-#2-007.reference_text:
210.52(C)(1) Wall Spaces
Receptacle outlets shall be installed so that no point along the wall line is more than 600 mm (24 in.) measured horizontally from a receptacle outlet in that space. The location of the receptacles shall be in accordance with 210.52(C)(3).
choice_notes: 10 inches is much closer than required; 210.52(C)(1) allows up to 600 mm (24 inches).
12 inches is the minimum countertop width that needs receptacles, not the 210.52(C)(1) spacing limit.
18 inches is not the countertop limit; 210.52(C)(1) allows up to 600 mm (24 inches).
210.52(C)(1) says no point along the countertop wall line may be more than 600 mm (24 inches) from a receptacle outlet.
open-book-exam-#2-007.tip_short: Countertop wall spaces: no point more than 24 inches from a receptacle, so a receptacle is needed at least every 4 feet. Correct: D — 24". 210.52(C)(1) says no point along the countertop wall line may be more than 600 mm (24 inches) from a receptacle outlet. Not A: 10 inches is much closer than required; 210.52(C)(1) allows up to 600 mm (24 inches). Not B: 12 inches is the minimum countertop width that needs receptacles, not the 210.52(C)(1) spacing limit. Not C: 18 inches is not the countertop limit; 210.52(C)(1) allows up to 600 mm (24 inches).

open-book-exam-#2-008.gist: Trees sway and grow, so temporary wiring hung from them needs hardware that gives with the movement. The question asks which devices the exception names besides tension take-up devices.
open-book-exam-#2-008.reference_text:
590.4(J) Support
Exception: For holiday lighting in accordance with 590.3(B), where the conductors or cables are arranged with strain relief devices, tension take-up devices, or other approved means to avoid damage from the movement of the live vegetation, trees shall be permitted to be used for support of overhead spans of branch-circuit conductors or cables.
choice_notes: Fittings are not named in the 590.4(J) exception; it lists strain relief or tension take-up devices.
Cable ties do not absorb tree movement; 590.4(J) calls for strain relief or tension take-up devices.
The 590.4(J) exception allows tree support where wiring has strain relief devices or tension take-up devices.
Overhead clamps hold wiring rigidly; 590.4(J) requires strain relief to absorb vegetation movement.
open-book-exam-#2-008.tip_short: Trees may hold holiday lighting spans only with strain relief or tension take-up devices so moving limbs do no harm. Correct: C — strain relief devices.
open-book-exam-#2-008.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: cable, conductors, temporary wiring. Start with 590.4(J), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#2-009.prompt: At least one 125 volt, single-phase, 15 or 20 amp rated receptacle outlet shall be installed within ___ of the top of each show window, and no point along the top of the window shall be farther than 6 feet from a receptacle outlet.
open-book-exam-#2-009.gist: Show window displays are lit and decorated from above, so receptacles belong near the top of the window. The question asks how close to the top of the window the receptacle must be.
open-book-exam-#2-009.reference_text:
210.62 Show Windows
At least one 125-volt, single-phase, 15- or 20-ampere-rated receptacle outlet shall be installed within 450 mm (18 in.) of the top of each show window. No point along the top of the window shall be farther than 1.8 m (6 ft) from a receptacle outlet.
choice_notes: 10 inches is closer than required; 210.62 allows the receptacle within 450 mm (18 inches) of the top.
12 inches is closer than required; 210.62 sets the limit at 450 mm (18 inches) from the top of the window.
210.62 requires the receptacle outlet within 450 mm (18 inches) of the top of each show window.
24 inches is too far; 210.62 requires the receptacle within 450 mm (18 inches) of the top of the window.
open-book-exam-#2-009.tip_short: Show window receptacles go within 18 inches of the top of the window, with no point along the top more than 6 feet from one. Correct: C — 18". 210.62 requires the receptacle outlet within 450 mm (18 inches) of the top of each show window. Not A: 10 inches is closer than required; 210.62 allows the receptacle within 450 mm (18 inches) of the top. Not B: 12 inches is closer than required; 210.62 sets the limit at 450 mm (18 inches) from the top of the window. Not D: 24 inches is too far; 210.62 requires the receptacle within 450 mm (18 inches) of the top of the window.

open-book-exam-#2-010.prompt: If festoon lighting is installed without a messenger, the smallest allowable overhead conductor is ___ AWG.
open-book-exam-#2-010.gist: String lighting hung overhead without a separate support wire has to carry its own weight, so the Code sets a minimum conductor size. The question asks the smallest size allowed.
open-book-exam-#2-010.reference_text:
225.6(B) Festoon Lighting
Overhead conductors for festoon lighting shall not be smaller than 12 AWG unless the conductors are supported by messenger wires. In all spans exceeding 12 m (40 ft), the conductors shall be supported by messenger wire. The messenger wire shall be supported by strain insulators.
choice_notes: #10 is allowed but is not the smallest; 225.6(B) permits down to 12 AWG without a messenger.
225.6(B) says festoon conductors shall not be smaller than 12 AWG unless supported by messenger wires.
#14 is smaller than the 12 AWG minimum 225.6(B) sets for festoon conductors without a messenger.
#16 is far below the 12 AWG minimum for overhead festoon conductors without a messenger.
open-book-exam-#2-010.tip_short: Festoon lighting without a messenger needs at least 12 AWG conductors, and any span over 40 feet always needs a messenger. Correct: B — #12. 225.6(B) says festoon conductors shall not be smaller than 12 AWG unless supported by messenger wires.

open-book-exam-#2-011.prompt: AFCI protection on all 120 volt, single-phase, 15 and 20 amp branch circuits in dwelling units supplying outlets is required in all of the following listed locations except ___.
open-book-exam-#2-011.gist: Dwelling AFCI protection covers a long list of living areas where cords and furniture can damage wiring. The question asks which pair of rooms is left off that list.
open-book-exam-#2-011.reference_text:
210.12(B) Dwelling Units
All 120-volt, single-phase, 10-, 15-, and 20-ampere branch circuits supplying outlets or devices installed in the following locations shall be protected by any of the means described in 210.12(A)(1) through (A)(6):
(1) Kitchens
(2) Family rooms
(3) Dining rooms
(4) Living rooms
(5) Parlors
(6) Libraries
(7) Dens
(8) Bedrooms
(9) Sunrooms
(10) Recreation rooms
(11) Closets
(12) Hallways
(13) Laundry areas
(14) Similar areas
choice_notes: Sunrooms, closets, and hallways are all listed in 210.12(B), so AFCI protection is required there.
Parlors, libraries, and dens are all listed in 210.12(B), so AFCI protection is required there.
Bathrooms and garages are not in the 210.12(B) list, so dwelling AFCI protection is not required there.
Living rooms, kitchens, and laundry areas are all listed in 210.12(B), so AFCI protection is required there.
open-book-exam-#2-011.tip_short: Dwelling AFCI covers kitchens, living areas, bedrooms, closets, hallways, and laundry areas; bathrooms and garages are not on the list. Correct: C — bathrooms and garages. Not A: Sunrooms, closets, and hallways are all listed in 210.12(B), so AFCI protection is required there. Not B: Parlors, libraries, and dens are all listed in 210.12(B), so AFCI protection is required there. Not D: Living rooms, kitchens, and laundry areas are all listed in 210.12(B), so AFCI protection is required there.

open-book-exam-#2-012.gist: Start from the table ampacity for the conductor's insulation, correct for ambient temperature if needed, then adjust for the number of current-carrying conductors in the raceway. The question asks the resulting ampacity.
open-book-exam-#2-012.reference_text:
Table 310.16 Ampacities of Insulated Conductors with Not More Than Three Current-Carrying Conductors in Raceway, Cable, or Earth (Directly Buried)
1. Section 310.15(B) shall be referenced for ampacity correction factors where the ambient temperature is other than 30°C (86°F).
2. Section 310.15(C)(1) shall be referenced for more than three current-carrying conductors.
Table 310.15(C)(1) Adjustment Factors for More Than Three Current-Carrying Conductors
4—6	80
7—9	70
reference_table: NOTE: Copper ampacities in amperes from Table 310.16. 86°F (30°C) ambient needs no correction (310.15(B)); 4 to 6 current-carrying conductors take 80 percent (Table 310.15(C)(1)).
choice_notes: 17.5 amperes uses the 70 percent factor for 7 to 9 conductors; four conductors take 80 percent.
#12 THWN is 25 amperes in the 75°C column of Table 310.16, 86°F needs no correction, and 25 times 0.80 is 20 amperes.
23 amperes matches no Table 310.15(C)(1) factor; 25 amperes times the 80 percent adjustment is 20 amperes.
26 amperes exceeds even the unadjusted 25 ampere rating; four conductors must be adjusted to 80 percent.
open-book-exam-#2-012.tip_short: THWN is a 75°C insulation: #12 copper is 25 amperes, 86°F needs no correction, and 4 to 6 current-carrying conductors take 80 percent. Correct: B — 20a. #12 THWN is 25 amperes in the 75°C column of Table 310.16, 86°F needs no correction, and 25 times 0.80 is 20 amperes. Not A: 17.5 amperes uses the 70 percent factor for 7 to 9 conductors; four conductors take 80 percent. Not C: 23 amperes matches no Table 310.15(C)(1) factor; 25 amperes times the 80 percent adjustment is 20 amperes. Not D: 26 amperes exceeds even the unadjusted 25 ampere rating; four conductors must be adjusted to 80 percent.
open-book-exam-#2-012.formula: Read the 75°C column of Table 310.16 for THWN, apply no temperature correction at 86°F, then multiply by the Table 310.15(C)(1) factor for four current-carrying conductors.

open-book-exam-#2-013.gist: An attached garage has a concrete floor where a person can be in contact with the earth. The question asks which protection a single receptacle for a fixed appliance there needs.
open-book-exam-#2-013.reference_text:
210.8(A) Dwelling Units
All 125-volt through 250-volt receptacles installed in the following locations and supplied by single-phase branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground shall have ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection for personnel:
(1) Bathrooms
(2) Garages and also accessory buildings that have a floor located at or below grade level not intended as habitable rooms and limited to storage areas, work areas, and areas of similar use
choice_notes: LCDI is cord protection for room air conditioners, not the personnel protection 210.8(A) requires.
210.8(A)(2) requires GFCI protection for garage receptacles, with no exception for a single appliance receptacle.
AFCI protects against arcing fires; the personnel protection 210.8(A)(2) requires for garage receptacles is GFCI.
Garages are not in the 210.12(B) AFCI list, so only GFCI protection is required for this receptacle.
open-book-exam-#2-013.tip_short: Every 125 through 250 volt receptacle in a dwelling garage needs GFCI, even a single one for a fixed appliance. Correct: B — GFCI. Not D: Garages are not in the 210.12(B) AFCI list, so only GFCI protection is required for this receptacle.

open-book-exam-#2-014.gist: A lockout hasp that is removable gets lost, and then the disconnect cannot be secured the next time someone works on the equipment. The question asks what may be present or absent while the locking provision stays in place.
open-book-exam-#2-014.reference_text:
110.25 Lockable Disconnecting Means
If a disconnecting means is required to be lockable open elsewhere in this Code, it shall be capable of being locked in the open position. The provisions for locking shall remain in place with or without the lock installed.
choice_notes: The cover is not the 110.25 wording; the locking provision must stay in place with or without the lock installed.
110.25 says the provisions for locking shall remain in place with or without the lock installed.
The switch is the disconnect itself, not what 110.25 refers to; the provision stays with or without the lock.
Device is not the 110.25 wording; the locking provision must remain with or without the lock installed.
open-book-exam-#2-014.tip_short: A lockable disconnect keeps its locking hardware in place whether or not a lock is on it. Correct: B — lock.

open-book-exam-#2-015.prompt: In a dwelling bedroom, wall space includes any space ___ or more in width (including space measured around corners) and unbroken along the floor line by doorways and similar openings, fireplaces, and fixed cabinets that do not have countertops or similar work surfaces.
open-book-exam-#2-015.gist: Dwelling bedrooms need receptacles along every wall space, and a stretch of wall counts only once it is wide enough. The question asks that minimum width.
open-book-exam-#2-015.reference_text:
210.52(A)(2) Wall Space
As used in this section, a wall space shall include the following:
