open-book-exam-#5-020.gist: Frost heave and settling soil can stretch a buried cable until it pulls apart or out of its fittings. The question asks how the cable should be laid to survive that movement.
open-book-exam-#5-020.reference_text:
300.5(J) Earth Movement
Where direct-buried conductors, raceways, or cables are subject to movement by settlement or frost, direct-buried conductors, raceways, or cables shall be arranged so as to prevent damage to the enclosed conductors or to equipment connected to the raceways.
Informational Note: This section recognizes "S" loops in underground direct burial cables and conductors to raceway transitions, expansion fittings in raceway risers to fixed equipment, and, generally, the provision of flexible connections to equipment subject to settlement or frost heaves.

Rod and pipe electrodes shall not be less than 2.44 m (8 ft) in length and consist of the following materials.

All switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards supplied by a feeder(s) in other than one- or two-family dwellings shall be permanently marked in accordance with the following:

open-book-exam-#5-025.prompt: Equipment grounding conductors, grounding electrode conductors, and bonding jumpers shall not be connected by ___.

250.8(A) Permitted Methods
Equipment grounding conductors, grounding electrode conductors, and bonding jumpers shall be connected by one or more of the following means:
(1) Listed pressure connectors
(2) Terminal bars
(3) Pressure connectors listed as grounding and bonding equipment
(4) Exothermic welding process
(5) Machine screw-type fasteners that engage not less than two threads or are secured with a nut
(6) Thread-forming machine screws that engage not less than two threads in the enclosure
(7) Connections that are part of a listed assembly
(8) Other listed means

The exothermic welding process is item (4) of the permitted methods in 250.8(A).

open-book-exam-#6-001.gist: Air in a return plenum is drawn through the whole building, so anything installed there must not feed a fire or give off toxic smoke. The question asks which wiring method is not allowed in that space.
open-book-exam-#6-001.reference_text:
300.22(C)(1) Wiring Methods
The wiring methods for other spaces used for environmental air shall be limited to totally enclosed, nonventilated, insulated busway having no provisions for plugin connections, Type MI cable without an overall nonmetallic covering, Type MC cable without an overall nonmetallic covering, Type AC cable, or other factory-assembled multiconductor control or power cable that is specifically listed for use within an air-handling space, or listed prefabricated cable assemblies of metallic manufactured wiring systems without nonmetallic sheath. Other types of cables, conductors, and raceways shall be permitted to be installed in electrical metallic tubing, flexible metallic tubing, intermediate metal conduit, rigid metal conduit without an overall nonmetallic covering, flexible metal conduit, or, where accessible, surface metal raceway or metal wireway with metal covers.
choice_notes: PVC is a nonmetallic raceway that burns and smokes; 300.22(C)(1) limits plenum raceways to metal types such as EMT, IMC, RMC and flexible metal conduit.
300.22(C)(1) permits Type MI cable without an overall nonmetallic covering in spaces used for environmental air.
300.22(C)(1) permits Type AC cable in other spaces used for environmental air.

open-book-exam-#6-001.tip_short: Plenum ceilings take metal: MI, MC and AC cable, EMT, IMC, RMC and flex; nonmetallic conduit such as PVC is not on the 300.22(C)(1) list. Correct: A — PVC. Not D: 300.22(C)(1) permits conductors in intermediate metal conduit in plenum spaces.

Article 100 defines ampacity as the maximum current a conductor can carry continuously without exceeding its temperature rating.
open-book-exam-#6-002.tip_short: Ampacity is the continuous current a conductor carries without exceeding its temperature rating (Article 100); heat is the limit. Correct: D — temperature.

open-book-exam-#6-005.prompt: Where overhead conductors not over 1,000 volts pass over a public driveway, they shall have a minimum clearance of not less than ___ feet above finished grade.

Overhead spans of open conductors and open multiconductor cables of not over 1000 volts, nominal, shall have a clearance of not less than the following:

(3) 4.5 m (15 ft) - for those areas listed in the 3.7 m (12 ft) classification where the voltage exceeds 300 volts to ground
(4) 5.5 m (18 ft) - over public streets, alleys, roads, parking areas subject to truck traffic, driveways on other than residential property, and other land traversed by vehicles, such as cultivated, grazing, forest, and orchard

It shall be driven to a depth of not less than 2.44 m (8 ft) except that, where rock bottom is encountered, the electrode shall be driven at an oblique angle not to exceed 45 degrees from the vertical or, where rock bottom is encountered at an angle up to 45 degrees, the electrode shall be permitted to be buried in a trench that is at least 750 mm (30 in.) deep.

open-book-exam-#6-007.gist: Meters, pilot lights and potential transformers in switchgear draw very little current, so their small wiring gets small overcurrent protection. The question asks the maximum rating of that protection.
open-book-exam-#6-007.reference_text:
408.52 Protection of Instrument Circuits
Instruments, pilot lights, voltage (potential) transformers, and other switchboard or switchgear devices with potential coils shall be supplied by a circuit that is protected by standard overcurrent devices rated 15 amperes or less.
Exception No. 1: Overcurrent devices rated more than 15 amperes shall be permitted where the interruption of the circuit could create a hazard. Short-circuit protection shall be provided.
Exception No. 2: For ratings of 2 amperes or less, special types of enclosed fuses shall be permitted.
choice_notes: 30 amperes is double the 408.52 limit of 15 amperes for instrument circuits.
20 amperes exceeds the 15-ampere limit in 408.52.
408.52 requires instrument, pilot light and potential coil circuits to be protected by standard overcurrent devices rated 15 amperes or less.
25 amperes exceeds the 15-ampere limit in 408.52.
open-book-exam-#6-007.tip_short: Switchboard instrument and pilot-light circuits: 15-ampere overcurrent devices or less, unless opening the circuit would create a hazard (408.52). Correct: C — 15.

open-book-exam-#6-008.gist: Where a direct-buried cable comes up out of the ground it can be hit by mowers, vehicles and people, so it is sleeved up the wall. The question asks how high that protection must reach.
open-book-exam-#6-008.reference_text:
300.5(D)(1) Emerging From Grade
Direct-buried conductors and cables emerging from grade and specified in Columns 1 and 4 of Table 300.5(A) shall be protected by enclosures or raceways extending from the minimum cover distance below grade required by 300.5(A) to a point at least 2.5 m (8 ft) above finished grade. In no case shall the protection be required to exceed 450 mm (18 in.) below finished grade.
choice_notes: 300.5(D)(1) requires protection extending to a point at least 2.5 m (8 feet) above finished grade.
10 feet is higher than the 8-foot requirement in 300.5(D)(1).
12 feet is higher than the 8-foot requirement in 300.5(D)(1).
22 inches is far too low; 300.5(D)(1) requires protection up to 8 feet above grade.
open-book-exam-#6-008.tip_short: Direct-buried cable coming out of the ground: protect it from the required cover depth up to 8 feet above grade, never more than 18 inches below (300.5(D)(1)). Correct: A — 8'. 300.5(D)(1) requires protection extending to a point at least 2.5 m (8 feet) above finished grade. Not B: 10 feet is higher than the 8-foot requirement in 300.5(D)(1). Not C: 12 feet is higher than the 8-foot requirement in 300.5(D)(1). Not D: 22 inches is far too low; 300.5(D)(1) requires protection up to 8 feet above grade.

open-book-exam-#6-009.prompt: Where the controller disconnecting means for a motor is not in sight of the motor, the following is required ___.
open-book-exam-#6-009.gist: A worker at a motor must be sure nobody can re-energize it from a distant controller disconnect he cannot see. The question asks what that out-of-sight disconnect must provide.
open-book-exam-#6-009.reference_text:
430.102(B)(2) Motor Controller Disconnect
The motor controller disconnecting means required in accordance with 430.102(A) shall be permitted to serve as the disconnecting means for the motor if it is in sight from the motor location and the driven machinery location.
Exception to (1) and (2): The disconnecting means for the motor shall not be required under either of the following conditions if the motor controller disconnecting means required in 430.102(A) is lockable in accordance with 110.25:
(1) Where such a location of the disconnecting means for the motor is impracticable or introduces additional or increased hazards to persons or property
(2) In industrial installations, with written safety procedures, where conditions of maintenance and supervision ensure that only qualified persons service the equipment
choice_notes: Moving the driven machinery is not a Code remedy; the 430.102(B) Exception requires the controller disconnect to be lockable.
The 430.102(B) Exception drops the motor disconnect only if the controller disconnecting means is lockable in accordance with 110.25, that is, capable of being locked open.
Accessibility alone does not protect a worker at a motor out of sight; the 430.102(B) Exception requires a lockable disconnect.
An isolating switch is not required here; the 430.102(B) Exception requires the controller disconnect to be lockable open.
open-book-exam-#6-009.tip_short: Motor out of sight of its controller disconnect (and no separate motor disconnect): the controller disconnect must be lockable open per 110.25 (430.102(B) Exception). Correct: B — the disconnecting means shall be lockable in the open position. The 430.102(B) Exception drops the motor disconnect only if the controller disconnecting means is lockable in accordance with 110.25, that is, capable of being locked open. Not A: Moving the driven machinery is not a Code remedy; the 430.102(B) Exception requires the controller disconnect to be lockable. Not C: Accessibility alone does not protect a worker at a motor out of sight; the 430.102(B) Exception requires a lockable disconnect. Not D: An isolating switch is not required here; the 430.102(B) Exception requires the controller disconnect to be lockable open.
open-book-exam-#6-009.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: motor, disconnecting means. Start with 430.102(B)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#6-010.prompt: What is the full load current of a 50 horsepower, three-phase, 480v, wound rotor, AC motor?
open-book-exam-#6-010.gist: Motor current comes from the Code's own table, never the nameplate, and a 480-volt system uses the 460-volt column. The question asks what a 50-horsepower wound-rotor motor reads there.
open-book-exam-#6-010.reference_text:
Table 430.250 Full-Load Current, Three-Phase Alternating-Current Motors
The following values of full-load currents are typical for motors running at speeds usual for belted motors and motors with normal torque characteristics. The voltages listed are rated motor voltages. The currents listed shall be permitted for system voltage ranges of 110 to 120, 220 to 240, 440 to 480, 550 to 600, and 2300 to 2400 volts.
Horsepower	Induction-Type Squirrel Cage and Wound Rotor (Amperes)	Synchronous-Type Unity Power Factor* (Amperes)
	115 Volts	200 Volts	208 Volts	230 Volts	460 Volts	575 Volts	2300 Volts	230 Volts	460 Volts	575 Volts	2300 Volts
40	-	120	114	104	52	41	-	83	41	33	-
50	-	150	143	130	65	52	-	104	52	42	-
choice_notes: 104 amperes is the synchronous-motor value at 230 volts, wrong on both motor type and voltage.
52 amperes is the synchronous-motor value for 50 horsepower at 460 volts, not the induction column.

41 amperes is the synchronous value for 40 horsepower at 460 volts, not a 50 horsepower induction motor.
open-book-exam-#6-010.tip_short: Three-phase motor full-load current comes from Table 430.250: find the horsepower row and the rated-voltage column (460 volts for a 480-volt system). Correct: C — 65 amps. Table 430.250 lists 65 amperes for a 50 horsepower induction-type (squirrel cage and wound rotor) motor in the 460 volt column. Not D: 41 amperes is the synchronous value for 40 horsepower at 460 volts, not a 50 horsepower induction motor.
open-book-exam-#6-010.formula: Read the full-load current straight from Table 430.250 for this horsepower and voltage.

open-book-exam-#6-011.gist: Someone replacing a fuse in a panelboard should be able to open a switch first so the fuse clips are dead. The question asks which side of the switch the fuses go on.
open-book-exam-#6-011.reference_text:
408.39 Relative Arrangement of Switches and Fuses
In panelboards, fuses of any type shall be installed on the load side of any switches.
Exception: Fuses installed as part of service equipment in accordance with the provisions of 230.94 shall be permitted on the line side of the service switch.
choice_notes: Positive is a dc polarity term, not a switch side; 408.39 puts fuses on the load side.
Negative is a dc polarity term, not a switch side; 408.39 puts fuses on the load side.
408.39 requires fuses of any type in panelboards to be installed on the load side of any switches.
Line-side fuses are allowed only as part of service equipment under the 408.39 Exception; the rule is load side.
open-book-exam-#6-011.tip_short: In panelboards the switch comes first and the fuses after it, on the load side, so opening the switch kills the fuses (408.39). Correct: C — load.

open-book-exam-#6-012.gist: The equipment grounding conductor is selected from its table using the upstream overcurrent device rating. A 50-amp breaker is given. The question asks the copper size across from it.
open-book-exam-#6-012.reference_text:
Table 250.122 Minimum Size Equipment Grounding Conductors for Grounding Raceway and Equipment
Rating or Setting of Automatic Overcurrent Device in Circuit Ahead of Equipment, Conduit, etc., Not Exceeding (Amperes)	Size (AWG or kcmil) Copper	Aluminum or Copper-Clad Aluminum
15	14	12
20	12	10
60	10	8
100	8	6
reference_table: NOTE: Size from the rating or setting of the overcurrent device ahead of the circuit, not from the circuit conductor size. A rating between rows uses the next larger row.
choice_notes: 14 AWG copper is the grounding conductor for a 15 ampere device, far too small for 50 amperes.
12 AWG copper is the grounding conductor for a 20 ampere device, too small for 50 amperes.
Table 250.122 requires 10 AWG copper for overcurrent devices up to 60 amperes, which covers 50 amperes.
8 AWG copper is the size for devices up to 100 amperes; 10 AWG copper is the minimum at 50 amperes.
open-book-exam-#6-012.tip_short: Size the equipment grounding conductor from Table 250.122 by the overcurrent device rating; a rating between rows takes the next larger row. Correct: C — #10. Table 250.122 requires 10 AWG copper for overcurrent devices up to 60 amperes, which covers 50 amperes. Not A: 14 AWG copper is the grounding conductor for a 15 ampere device, far too small for 50 amperes. Not B: 12 AWG copper is the grounding conductor for a 20 ampere device, too small for 50 amperes. Not D: 8 AWG copper is the size for devices up to 100 amperes; 10 AWG copper is the minimum at 50 amperes.
open-book-exam-#6-012.formula: Size the EGC from Table 250.122 using the branch-circuit rating.

open-book-exam-#6-013.gist: Flexible liquidtight conduit can pull out of its fittings if it is left to hang, so it must be fastened close to each termination. The question asks the maximum distance to that fastener.
open-book-exam-#6-013.reference_text:
350.30(A) Securely Fastened
LFMC shall be securely fastened in place by an approved means within 300 mm (12 in.) of each box, cabinet, conduit body, or other conduit termination and shall be supported and secured at intervals not to exceed 1.4 m (4 1/2 ft). Where used, cable ties shall be listed and be identified for securement and support.
choice_notes: 8 inches is closer than required; 350.30(A) allows up to 12 inches.
350.30(A) requires LFMC to be securely fastened within 300 mm (12 inches) of each box, cabinet, conduit body or other termination.
16 inches exceeds the 12-inch limit in 350.30(A).
24 inches is double the 12-inch limit in 350.30(A).
open-book-exam-#6-013.tip_short: LFMC: fasten within 12 inches of each termination and at least every 4 1/2 feet (350.30(A)), the same as FMC. Correct: B — 12". 350.30(A) requires LFMC to be securely fastened within 300 mm (12 inches) of each box, cabinet, conduit body or other termination. Not A: 8 inches is closer than required; 350.30(A) allows up to 12 inches. Not C: 16 inches exceeds the 12-inch limit in 350.30(A). Not D: 24 inches is double the 12-inch limit in 350.30(A).

open-book-exam-#6-014.prompt: Conduit nipples not over 24 inches in length may be filled to a maximum of ___ of their CSA.
open-book-exam-#6-014.gist: A short conduit section between enclosures permits a higher fill percentage than a complete conduit run. The question asks how full, as a percent.
open-book-exam-#6-014.reference_text:
Chapter 9 Notes to Tables, Note (4)
Where conduit or tubing nipples, not including connectors, having a maximum length not to exceed 600 mm (24 in.) are installed between boxes, cabinets, and similar enclosures, the nipples shall be permitted to be filled to 60 percent of their total cross-sectional area, and 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors need not apply to this condition.
reference_table: NOTE: Fill is of total cross-sectional area; connectors are not counted; 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors need not apply.
choice_notes: 50 percent is not a Chapter 9 fill limit; nipples 24 inches or less allow 60 percent.
Chapter 9 Note 4 permits 60 percent fill for nipples not over 600 mm (24 inches).
70 percent exceeds the 60 percent allowed for nipples.
80 percent exceeds the 60 percent allowed for nipples.
open-book-exam-#6-014.tip_short: Nipples 24 inches or shorter between enclosures may be filled to 60 percent, with no adjustment factors (Chapter 9, Note 4). Correct: B — 60%. Chapter 9 Note 4 permits 60 percent fill for nipples not over 600 mm (24 inches). Not A: 50 percent is not a Chapter 9 fill limit; nipples 24 inches or less allow 60 percent. Not C: 70 percent exceeds the 60 percent allowed for nipples. Not D: 80 percent exceeds the 60 percent allowed for nipples.
open-book-exam-#6-014.formula: Nipples 24 in. or shorter use the nipple fill note instead of Table 1 (Chapter 9, Note 4).

open-book-exam-#6-015.gist: Underground raceways collect groundwater and condensation no matter how well they are sealed. The question asks how the Code classifies the inside of those raceways.
open-book-exam-#6-015.reference_text:
300.5(B) Wet Locations
The interior of enclosures or raceways installed underground shall be considered to be a wet location. Insulated conductors and cables installed in these enclosures or raceways in underground installations shall comply with 310.10(C).
choice_notes: Buried is not an NEC location classification; 300.5(B) calls the interior a wet location.
Isolated is not a moisture classification; 300.5(B) calls the interior a wet location.
Damp understates the condition; 300.5(B) treats the interior of underground raceways as a wet location.
300.5(B) states that the interior of enclosures or raceways installed underground shall be considered to be a wet location.
open-book-exam-#6-015.tip_short: Anything inside an underground raceway or enclosure is in a wet location, so the conductors must be wet-rated (300.5(B), 310.10(C)). Correct: D — wet.

open-book-exam-#6-016.prompt: Rigid PVC, size 1 1/2 inch, shall be supported every ___.
open-book-exam-#6-016.gist: PVC sags between supports, especially when warm, so the Code sets a support spacing that grows with trade size. The question asks the spacing for 1 1/2-inch conduit.

open-book-exam-#6-017.gist: Flat conductor cable runs under carpet squares, so its circuits are kept small. The Code sets one limit for general-purpose circuits and a higher one for individual circuits. The question asks the individual branch-circuit limit.
open-book-exam-#6-017.reference_text:
324.10(B)(2) Current
General-purpose and appliance branch circuits shall have ratings not exceeding 20 amperes. Individual branch circuits shall have ratings not exceeding 30 amperes.
choice_notes: 324.10(B)(2) permits individual FCC branch circuits with ratings not exceeding 30 amperes.
25 amperes is not a limit in 324.10(B)(2); individual branch circuits may be rated up to 30 amperes.
20 amperes is the 324.10(B)(2) limit for general-purpose and appliance circuits, not individual branch circuits.
15 amperes is not the 324.10(B)(2) limit; individual branch circuits may be rated up to 30 amperes.
open-book-exam-#6-017.tip_short: FCC under carpet: general-purpose and appliance circuits 20 amperes maximum, individual branch circuits 30 amperes maximum (324.10(B)(2)). Correct: A — 30 amps. 324.10(B)(2) permits individual FCC branch circuits with ratings not exceeding 30 amperes. Not B: 25 amperes is not a limit in 324.10(B)(2); individual branch circuits may be rated up to 30 amperes. Not C: 20 amperes is the 324.10(B)(2) limit for general-purpose and appliance circuits, not individual branch circuits. Not D: 15 amperes is not the 324.10(B)(2) limit; individual branch circuits may be rated up to 30 amperes.

open-book-exam-#6-018.prompt: A battery room where batteries are being charged requires ventilation to prevent ___.
open-book-exam-#6-018.gist: Some batteries give off hydrogen while they charge, and hydrogen trapped in a closed room is a serious hazard. The question asks what the required ventilation prevents.
open-book-exam-#6-018.reference_text:
480.10(A) Ventilation
Provisions appropriate to the battery technology shall be made for sufficient diffusion and ventilation of gases from the battery, if present, to prevent the accumulation of an explosive mixture.
choice_notes: Corrosion is handled by other means; 480.10(A) ventilation prevents the accumulation of an explosive mixture.
Electrostatic charge is not the concern of 480.10(A); ventilation disperses gases to prevent an explosive mixture.
Acid corrosion is not what 480.10(A) addresses; ventilation prevents an explosive gas mixture.
480.10(A) requires diffusion and ventilation of battery gases, if present, to prevent the accumulation of an explosive mixture.
open-book-exam-#6-018.tip_short: Battery ventilation exists to keep charging gases such as hydrogen from building up into an explosive mixture (480.10(A)). Correct: D — an explosive mixture.

open-book-exam-#6-019.prompt: A single ground rod that does not have a resistance to ground of 25 ohms or less can be supplemented by which of the following?
open-book-exam-#6-019.gist: One driven rod alone is rarely a good connection to earth, so unless it tests at 25 ohms or less it needs a partner electrode. The question asks which electrode types can serve as that supplement.
open-book-exam-#6-019.reference_text:
250.53(A)(2) Supplemental Electrode Required
A single rod, pipe, or plate electrode shall be supplemented by an additional electrode of a type specified in 250.52(A)(2) through (A)(8). The supplemental electrode shall be permitted to be bonded to one of the following:
(1) Rod, pipe, or plate electrode
(2) Grounding electrode conductor
(3) Grounded service-entrance conductor
(4) Nonflexible grounded service raceway
(5) Any grounded service enclosure
Exception: If a single rod, pipe, or plate grounding electrode has a resistance to earth of 25 ohms or less, the supplemental electrode shall not be required.
choice_notes: A ground ring, 250.52(A)(4), qualifies, but so do the other listed types, so it is not the only answer.
A concrete-encased electrode, 250.52(A)(3), qualifies, but so do the other listed types.
A metal in-ground support structure, 250.52(A)(2), qualifies, but so do the other listed types.
250.53(A)(2) allows any electrode type in 250.52(A)(2) through (A)(8), which includes all three choices.
open-book-exam-#6-019.tip_short: A lone rod needs a supplemental electrode of any type in 250.52(A)(2) through (A)(8), unless it measures 25 ohms or less (250.53(A)(2)). Correct: D — Any of these. 250.53(A)(2) allows any electrode type in 250.52(A)(2) through (A)(8), which includes all three choices. Not B: A concrete-encased electrode, 250.52(A)(3), qualifies, but so do the other listed types.
open-book-exam-#6-019.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 250.53(A)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#6-020.gist: Every hole cut for a cable or conduit in a fire-rated wall or floor is a path for fire and smoke unless it is sealed properly. The question asks which Code term describes the required firestop methods.
open-book-exam-#6-020.reference_text:
300.21 Spread of Fire or Products of Combustion
Electrical installations in hollow spaces, vertical shafts, and ventilation or air-handling ducts shall be made so that the possible spread of fire or products of combustion will not be substantially increased. Openings around electrical penetrations into or through fire-resistant-rated walls, partitions, floors, or ceilings shall be firestopped using approved methods to maintain the fire resistance rating.
choice_notes: Suitable is not the word in 300.21; the firestop methods must be approved.
Listed firestop systems are common, but 300.21 requires approved methods, meaning acceptable to the AHJ.
Identified is a different defined term; 300.21 requires approved methods.
300.21 requires openings around penetrations of fire-resistant-rated construction to be firestopped using approved methods.
open-book-exam-#6-020.tip_short: Penetrations of fire-rated walls, floors and ceilings must be firestopped by approved methods, meaning acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction (300.21). Correct: D — approved.

open-book-exam-#6-021.gist: Small snap switches in a panelboard cannot withstand a large fault, so the panel feeding them has a limit on its overcurrent protection. The question asks that limit.
open-book-exam-#6-021.reference_text:
408.36(A) Snap Switches Rated at 30 Amperes or Less
Panelboards equipped with snap switches rated at 30 amperes or less shall have overcurrent protection of 200 amperes or less.
choice_notes: 30 amperes is the snap switch rating in the rule, not the panelboard protection limit of 200 amperes in 408.36(A).
60 amperes is not the 408.36(A) limit; the panelboard protection may be up to 200 amperes.
100 amperes is not the 408.36(A) limit; the panelboard protection may be up to 200 amperes.
408.36(A) requires panelboards with snap switches rated 30 amperes or less to have overcurrent protection of 200 amperes or less.
open-book-exam-#6-021.tip_short: A panelboard with snap switches of 30 amperes or less must be protected at 200 amperes or less (408.36(A)). Correct: D — 200.

open-book-exam-#6-022.prompt: Type MC cable shall be permitted to be unsupported and unsecured where the cable is not more than ___ in length from the last point of cable support to the point of connection to luminaires within an accessible ceiling.
open-book-exam-#6-022.gist: A short unsupported whip of MC cable from the last support to a lay-in luminaire is allowed in an accessible ceiling so the fixture can be moved. The question asks the maximum length of that whip.
open-book-exam-#6-022.reference_text:
330.30(D) Unsupported Cables
Type MC cable shall be permitted to be unsupported and unsecured where the cable complies with any of the following:
(1) Is fished between access points through concealed spaces in finished buildings or structures and supporting is impractical
(2) Is not more than 1.8 m (6 ft) in length from the last point of cable support to the point of connection to luminaires or other electrical equipment and the cable and point of connection are within an accessible ceiling
(3) Is Type MC of the interlocked armor type in lengths not exceeding 900 mm (3 ft) from the last point where it is securely fastened and is used to connect equipment where flexibility is necessary to minimize the transmission of vibration from equipment or to provide flexibility for equipment that requires movement after installation
choice_notes: 36 inches (3 feet) is the 330.30(D)(3) limit for interlocked MC used for flexibility, not luminaire whips.
48 inches is shorter than the 6 feet 330.30(D)(2) allows for luminaire connections.
60 inches is shorter than the 6 feet 330.30(D)(2) allows for luminaire connections.
330.30(D)(2) permits up to 1.8 m (6 feet, or 72 inches) unsupported from the last point of cable support to a luminaire within an accessible ceiling.
open-book-exam-#6-022.tip_short: MC whips to luminaires in an accessible ceiling may run unsupported up to 6 feet from the last support; interlocked MC for flexibility up to 3 feet (330.30(D)). Correct: D — 72". 330.30(D)(2) permits up to 1.8 m (6 feet, or 72 inches) unsupported from the last point of cable support to a luminaire within an accessible ceiling. Not A: 36 inches (3 feet) is the 330.30(D)(3) limit for interlocked MC used for flexibility, not luminaire whips. Not B: 48 inches is shorter than the 6 feet 330.30(D)(2) allows for luminaire connections. Not C: 60 inches is shorter than the 6 feet 330.30(D)(2) allows for luminaire connections.

open-book-exam-#6-023.gist: Underground wiring close to a pool sits in soaked soil near people in the water, so only certain raceways and cables are allowed in that zone. The question asks how far out from the pool wall that zone extends.
open-book-exam-#6-023.reference_text:
680.11(A) Underground Wiring
Underground wiring within 1.5 m (5 ft) horizontally from the inside wall of the pool shall be permitted. The following wiring methods shall be considered suitable for the conditions in these locations provided they are installed complete between outlets, junctions, or splicing points:
(1) Rigid metal conduit
(2) Intermediate metal conduit
(3) Rigid polyvinyl chloride conduit
(4) Reinforced thermosetting resin conduit
(5) Jacketed Type MC cable that is listed for burial use
(6) Liquidtight flexible nonmetallic conduit listed for direct burial use
(7) Liquidtight flexible metal conduit listed for direct burial use
choice_notes: 18 inches is not the 680.11(A) distance; the zone extends 5 feet from the inside wall of the pool.
24 inches is not the 680.11(A) distance; the zone extends 5 feet from the inside wall of the pool.
48 inches is short of the 5-foot (60-inch) zone in 680.11(A).
680.11(A) covers underground wiring within 1.5 m (5 feet, or 60 inches) horizontally from the inside wall of the pool.
open-book-exam-#6-023.tip_short: Underground wiring within 5 feet of the inside pool wall must use one of the seven methods in 680.11(A), including LFMC listed for direct burial. Correct: D — 60". 680.11(A) covers underground wiring within 1.5 m (5 feet, or 60 inches) horizontally from the inside wall of the pool. Not A: 18 inches is not the 680.11(A) distance; the zone extends 5 feet from the inside wall of the pool. Not B: 24 inches is not the 680.11(A) distance; the zone extends 5 feet from the inside wall of the pool. Not C: 48 inches is short of the 5-foot (60-inch) zone in 680.11(A).
open-book-exam-#6-023.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: conduit, pool / spa. Start with 680.11(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#6-024.gist: A branch circuit needs one number that everything else on it is matched to, even if the wire is oversized for voltage drop. The question asks what sets that rating.
open-book-exam-#6-024.reference_text:
210.18 Rating
Branch circuits recognized by this article shall be rated in accordance with the maximum permitted ampere rating or setting of the overcurrent device. The rating for other than individual branch circuits shall be 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amperes. Where conductors of higher ampacity are used for any reason, the ampere rating or setting of the specified overcurrent device shall determine the circuit rating.
choice_notes: Receptacle ratings must match the circuit, but 210.18 rates the circuit by the overcurrent device.
210.18 rates branch circuits by the maximum permitted ampere rating or setting of the overcurrent device.
The number of outlets does not set the rating; 210.18 uses the overcurrent device rating.
210.18 says oversized conductors do not change the rating; the overcurrent device determines it.
open-book-exam-#6-024.tip_short: A branch circuit is rated by its overcurrent device, not its wire or receptacles; oversized conductors do not raise the rating (210.18). Correct: B — maximum permitted rating of the fuse or breaker. 210.18 rates branch circuits by the maximum permitted ampere rating or setting of the overcurrent device. Not A: Receptacle ratings must match the circuit, but 210.18 rates the circuit by the overcurrent device. Not C: The number of outlets does not set the rating; 210.18 uses the overcurrent device rating. Not D: 210.18 says oversized conductors do not change the rating; the overcurrent device determines it.

open-book-exam-#6-025.gist: Intrinsically safe wiring must never be mixed up with ordinary wiring in a hazardous area, and a unique color makes it easy to spot. The question asks which color the Code reserves for it.
open-book-exam-#6-025.reference_text:
504.80(C) Color Coding
Color coding shall be permitted to identify intrinsically safe conductors where they are colored light blue and where no other conductors colored light blue are used.

Purple is not the 504.80(C) color; intrinsically safe conductors may be colored light blue.
open-book-exam-#6-025.tip_short: Intrinsically safe conductors may be identified by light blue, as long as no other conductors are light blue (504.80(C)). Correct: B — light blue.

open-book-exam-#9-001.gist: Concealed knob-and-tube conductors run open on insulators inside walls and ceilings, so air space keeps them apart. The question asks the minimum spacing between the conductors.
open-book-exam-#9-001.reference_text:
394.19(A) General
A clearance of not less than 75 mm (3 in.) shall be maintained between conductors and a clearance of not less than 25 mm (1 in.) between the conductor and the surface over which it passes.
choice_notes: 2 inches is too little; 394.19(A) requires at least 3 inches between conductors.
394.19(A) requires a clearance of not less than 75 mm (3 inches) between conductors.
4 inches is more than the minimum; 394.19(A) requires only 3 inches between conductors.
6 inches is double the 3-inch minimum that 394.19(A) sets between conductors.
open-book-exam-#9-001.tip_short: Concealed knob-and-tube: 3 inches between conductors and 1 inch from the surface they pass over. Correct: B — 3". 394.19(A) requires a clearance of not less than 75 mm (3 inches) between conductors. Not A: 2 inches is too little; 394.19(A) requires at least 3 inches between conductors. Not C: 4 inches is more than the minimum; 394.19(A) requires only 3 inches between conductors. Not D: 6 inches is double the 3-inch minimum that 394.19(A) sets between conductors.

open-book-exam-#9-002.gist: Article 250 has several sizing tables, each for a different kind of grounding or bonding conductor. The question asks which table sizes the equipment grounding conductor run with a circuit.
open-book-exam-#9-002.reference_text:
Table 250.122 Minimum Size Equipment Grounding Conductors for Grounding Raceway and Equipment
Copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum equipment grounding conductors of the wire type shall not be smaller than shown in Table 250.122.
choice_notes: Table 250.66 sizes the grounding electrode conductor from the service conductor size, not the equipment grounding conductor.
Table 250.94 covers the intersystem bonding and the bonding conductor for communication systems, not equipment grounding conductors.
Table 250.102(C)(1) sizes the grounded conductor, main bonding jumper, system bonding jumper, and supply-side bonding jumper.
Table 250.122 gives the minimum size equipment grounding conductor based on the rating or setting of the overcurrent device.
open-book-exam-#9-002.tip_short: Equipment grounding conductors are sized from Table 250.122 by the rating of the overcurrent device ahead of the circuit. Correct: D — 250.122.

open-book-exam-#9-003.prompt: Informational Note: ANSI ___-2017, Product Safety Signs and Labels, provides guidelines for suitable font sizes, words, colors, symbols, and location requirements for labels.
open-book-exam-#9-003.gist: Field-applied warning labels must use effective words, colors, and symbols, and an informational note points to an ANSI standard for the details. The question asks the number of that product safety sign and label standard.
open-book-exam-#9-003.reference_text:
110.21(B) Field-Applied Hazard Markings
Where caution, warning, or danger hazard markings such as labels or signs are required by this Code, the markings shall meet the following requirements:
The marking shall be of sufficient durability to withstand the environment involved and warn of the hazards using effective words, colors, symbols, or any combination thereof.
Informational Note No. 2: See ANSI Z535.4-2011 (R2017), Product Safety Signs and Labels, which details the design, application, use, and placement of safety signs and labels on a wide variety of products.
choice_notes: 110.21(B) Informational Note No. 2 cites this ANSI standard (2011, reaffirmed 2017), Product Safety Signs and Labels.
Z541.B is not the standard cited in 110.21(B); product safety labels are in the ANSI Z535 family.
Z212.W is not a standard referenced in 110.21(B) for hazard markings.
Z1956.G is not an ANSI standard cited by the NEC for hazard markings in 110.21(B).
open-book-exam-#9-003.tip_short: Field-applied hazard labels point to the ANSI Z535 safety-sign family; its part 4 covers product safety signs and labels. Correct: A — Z535.4. 110.21(B) Informational Note No. 2 cites this ANSI standard (2011, reaffirmed 2017), Product Safety Signs and Labels.
open-book-exam-#9-003.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 110.21(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#9-004.prompt: Where there is equipment for more than one elevator car in the machine room, the heating and air-conditioning disconnecting means shall be numbered to correspond to the identifying number of the elevator car that they control. The disconnecting means shall be provided with a sign to identify the ___ of the supply side overcurrent protective device.
open-book-exam-#9-004.gist: Elevator disconnects in a shared machine room are numbered by car, and a sign tells workers where to find the protective device feeding each one. The question asks what that sign must identify about the supply side overcurrent device.
open-book-exam-#9-004.reference_text:
620.54 Heating and Air-Conditioning Disconnecting Means
Where there is equipment for more than one elevator car in the machine room, the disconnecting means shall be numbered to correspond to the identifying number of the elevator car whose heating and air-conditioning source they control.
The disconnecting means shall be provided with a sign to identify the location of the supply side overcurrent protective device.
choice_notes: The sign is not for amperage; 620.54 requires it to identify the location of the supply side overcurrent device.
The load is not what the sign shows; 620.54 requires the location of the supply side overcurrent device.
620.54 requires a sign to identify the location of the supply side overcurrent protective device.
Voltage is not the required content; 620.54 requires a sign identifying the location of the supply side device.
open-book-exam-#9-004.tip_short: Elevator disconnecting means carry a sign that tells where the supply side overcurrent device is, so a worker can find it fast. Correct: C — location.
open-book-exam-#9-004.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: overcurrent protection, load calculation, disconnecting means. Start with 620.54, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#9-005.gist: Chapter 9 holds several tables used together for raceway fill: one for the allowed fill percentage, others for raceway areas, conductor areas, and conductor properties. The question asks which one gives the allowed fill percentage.

Chapter 9, Table 1 Percent of Cross Section of Conduit and Tubing for Conductors and Cables
Number of Conductors and/or Cables	Cross-Sectional Area (%)
1	53
2	31
Over 2	40

Chapter 9 Table 8 gives conductor properties such as area and resistance, not fill percentages.
Chapter 9 Table 1 lists the percent of cross section of conduit and tubing for conductors and cables.
Chapter 9 Table 5 gives dimensions of insulated conductors and fixture wires, not fill percentages.
open-book-exam-#9-005.tip_short: Chapter 9 Table 1 sets the fill percentage: 53 percent for one conductor, 31 percent for two, 40 percent for over two. Correct: C — Table 1, Chapter 9. Chapter 9 Table 1 lists the percent of cross section of conduit and tubing for conductors and cables. Not A: Chapter 9 Table 4 gives the dimensions and usable areas of conduit and tubing, not the fill percentages. Not B: Chapter 9 Table 8 gives conductor properties such as area and resistance, not fill percentages. Not D: Chapter 9 Table 5 gives dimensions of insulated conductors and fixture wires, not fill percentages.

open-book-exam-#9-006.gist: Below 800 amperes the Code lets you round up to the next standard device size, but above 800 amperes that allowance ends. The question asks how the conductor ampacity must compare with the device rating.
open-book-exam-#9-006.reference_text:
240.4(C) Overcurrent Devices Rated Over 800 Amperes
Where the overcurrent device is rated over 800 amperes, the ampacity of the conductors it protects shall be equal to or greater than the rating of the overcurrent device defined in 240.6.
choice_notes: 80 percent would leave the conductors smaller than the device; 240.4(C) requires equal to or greater than.
100 percent is close, but 240.4(C) uses the words equal to or greater than the device rating.
240.4(C) requires the conductor ampacity to be equal to or greater than the rating of the overcurrent device.
Not less than means the same in practice, but the wording in 240.4(C) is equal to or greater than.
open-book-exam-#9-006.tip_short: Over 800 amperes there is no next-size-up allowance: the conductor ampacity must equal or exceed the overcurrent device rating. Correct: C — equal to or greater than. Not A: 80 percent would leave the conductors smaller than the device; 240.4(C) requires equal to or greater than. Not B: 100 percent is close, but 240.4(C) uses the words equal to or greater than the device rating.

open-book-exam-#9-007.gist: Cutting threads in the field strips the factory zinc coating, so the bare threads need a protective compound that still conducts. The question asks which acceptance term the Code uses for that compound.
open-book-exam-#9-007.reference_text:
300.6(A) Ferrous Metal Equipment
Where corrosion protection is necessary and the conduit is threaded anywhere other than at the factory where the product is listed, the threads shall be coated with an approved electrically conductive, corrosion-resistant compound.
choice_notes: 300.6(A) requires field-cut threads to be coated with an approved electrically conductive, corrosion-resistant compound.
UL Listed is not the NEC term used in 300.6(A); the compound must be approved.
Identified is a different defined term; 300.6(A) uses approved for the thread compound.
Labeled is not the requirement in 300.6(A); the compound must be approved by the AHJ.
open-book-exam-#9-007.tip_short: Field-cut threads on ferrous conduit get an approved electrically conductive, corrosion-resistant compound; approved means acceptable to the AHJ. Correct: A — Approved.

open-book-exam-#9-008.prompt: A permanent and legible ___ diagram of the local switching arrangement, clearly identifying each point of connection to the high-voltage section, shall be provided within sight of each point of connection.
open-book-exam-#9-008.gist: Where high-voltage equipment could be backfed, workers need a drawing at each connection point that shows how the switching is arranged. The question asks what kind of diagram is required.
open-book-exam-#9-008.reference_text:
495.25(B) Diagram
A permanent and legible single-line diagram of the local switching arrangement, clearly identifying each point of connection to the high-voltage section, shall be provided within sight of each point of connection.
choice_notes: A schematic is not the term used; 495.25(B) requires a single-line diagram of the local switching arrangement.
A riser diagram is not what 495.25(B) requires; it calls for a single-line diagram.
495.25(B) requires a permanent and legible single-line diagram of the local switching arrangement.
A connection diagram is not the required type; 495.25(B) specifies a single-line diagram.
open-book-exam-#9-008.tip_short: Backfeed on over-1000-volt equipment: post a permanent single-line diagram of the switching within sight of each connection point. Correct: C — single-line.

open-book-exam-#9-009.prompt: For motors marked with design letters B, C, or D, conductors having a higher insulation rating shall be permitted to be used, provided the ampacity of such conductors does not exceed the ___ ampacity.
open-book-exam-#9-009.gist: Small circuits normally use the 60°C column for terminations, but motors with certain design letters get an exception. The question asks which temperature column caps the conductor ampacity for those motors.
open-book-exam-#9-009.reference_text:
110.14(C)(1) Equipment Provisions
Termination provisions of equipment for circuits rated 100 amperes or less, or marked for 14 AWG through 1 AWG conductors, shall be used only for one of the following:
For motors marked with design letters B, C, or D, conductors having an insulation rating of 75°C (167°F) or higher shall be permitted to be used, provided the ampacity of such conductors does not exceed the 75°C (167°F) ampacity.
choice_notes: 60°C is the general limit for 100-ampere-or-less terminations; design B, C, or D motors may use the 75°C ampacity.
110.14(C)(1)(a)(4) permits 75°C or higher insulated conductors for design B, C, or D motors at the 75°C ampacity.
90°C ampacity may be used only for adjustment and correction, not as the termination ampacity here.
104°C is not a termination rating in 110.14(C); the limit for these motors is the 75°C ampacity.
open-book-exam-#9-009.tip_short: Design B, C, or D motors on circuits of 100 amperes or less may use 75°C conductors at their 75°C ampacity, not the usual 60°C limit. Correct: B — 75°C.
open-book-exam-#9-009.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ampacity, conductors, motor. Start with 110.14(C)(1), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#9-010.gist: A sign with incandescent lampholders must tell whoever relamps it the maximum wattage per lampholder, so the marking has a minimum letter size. The question asks how tall the letters must be.
open-book-exam-#9-010.reference_text:
600.4(C) Signs With Lampholders for Incandescent Lamps
Signs and outline lighting systems with lampholders for incandescent lamps shall be marked to indicate the maximum allowable lamp wattage per lampholder. The markings shall be permanently installed, in letters at least 6 mm (1/4 in.) high, and shall be located where visible during relamping.
choice_notes: 600.4(C) requires the lamp wattage marking in letters at least 6 mm (1/4 inch) high.
1/2 inch is larger than required; 600.4(C) sets a minimum letter height of 1/4 inch.
1 inch is four times the 1/4-inch minimum letter height in 600.4(C).
2 inches is far larger than the 1/4-inch minimum letter height in 600.4(C).
open-book-exam-#9-010.tip_short: Sign lampholder wattage markings: permanent, at least 1/4-inch letters, visible during relamping. Correct: A — 1/4". 600.4(C) requires the lamp wattage marking in letters at least 6 mm (1/4 inch) high. Not B: 1/2 inch is larger than required; 600.4(C) sets a minimum letter height of 1/4 inch. Not C: 1 inch is four times the 1/4-inch minimum letter height in 600.4(C). Not D: 2 inches is far larger than the 1/4-inch minimum letter height in 600.4(C).

open-book-exam-#9-011.gist: Motor branch circuits get their fuse or breaker size from a table of percentages of motor full-load current. The question asks the number of that table.
open-book-exam-#9-011.reference_text:
Table 430.52(C)(1) Maximum Rating or Setting of Motor Branch-Circuit Short-Circuit and Ground-Fault Protective Devices
A protective device that has a rating or setting not exceeding the value calculated according to the values given in Table 430.52(C)(1) shall be used unless otherwise permitted in 430.52(C)(1)(a) or (C)(1)(b).
choice_notes: Table 430.248 gives full-load currents of single-phase motors, not protective device ratings.
Table 430.52(C)(1) lists the maximum rating or setting of motor branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protective devices.
Table 430.37 lists the number and location of overload units, not short-circuit device ratings.
430.22 covers conductor sizing for a single motor; Table 430.22(E) is duty-cycle sizing, not protective devices.
open-book-exam-#9-011.tip_short: Motor short-circuit and ground-fault protection is sized with Table 430.52(C)(1) percentages of the motor full-load current. Correct: B — 430.52(C)(1).
open-book-exam-#9-011.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ground fault, motor. Start with Table 430.52(C)(1), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#9-012.gist: A branch circuit takes its rating from the protective device, not from the wire. Adjustable breakers make a second word necessary. The question asks that word.
open-book-exam-#9-012.reference_text:
210.18 Rating
Branch circuits recognized by this article shall be rated in accordance with the maximum permitted ampere rating or setting of the overcurrent device.
choice_notes: Listing is not what rates a branch circuit; 210.18 uses the rating or setting of the overcurrent device.
Marking is not the word in 210.18; the circuit is rated by the device's rating or setting.
210.18 rates branch circuits by the maximum permitted ampere rating or setting of the overcurrent device.
Rating is already in the stem; 210.18 says rating or setting of the overcurrent device.
open-book-exam-#9-012.tip_short: A branch circuit is rated by the ampere rating or setting of its overcurrent device, not by its conductor size. Correct: C — setting.

open-book-exam-#9-013.prompt: Ventilating pipes for motors, generators, or other rotating electrical machinery, or for enclosures for electrical equipment, shall be of metal not less than .021 inch in thickness or of equally substantial noncombustible material and shall comply with: ___.
open-book-exam-#9-013.gist: In a Class II combustible dust location, ventilating pipes for motors and enclosures must carry clean air and survive their environment. The question asks which listed requirement the pipes must meet.
open-book-exam-#9-013.reference_text:
502.128 Ventilating Piping
Ventilating pipes for motors, generators, or other rotating electrical machinery, or for enclosures for electrical equipment, shall be of metal not less than 0.53 mm (0.021 in.) in thickness or of equally substantial noncombustible material and shall comply with all of the following:
Lead directly to a source of clean air outside of buildings
Be screened at the outer ends to prevent the entrance of small animals or birds
Be protected against physical damage and against rusting or other corrosive influences
choice_notes: 502.128 sets no 360-degree bend limit for ventilating pipes; that is a raceway rule elsewhere.
502.128(1) requires the pipes to lead to a source of clean air outside of buildings, not into attic space.
502.128(3) requires ventilating pipes to be protected against physical damage and against rusting or other corrosive influences.
502.128(2) requires the outer ends to be screened against small animals or birds, not fitted with hinged openings.
open-book-exam-#9-013.tip_short: Class II ventilating pipes: lead to clean outside air, be screened at the outer ends, and be protected against damage and corrosion. Correct: C — be protected against physical damage and against rusting or other corrosive influences. Not A: 502.128 sets no 360-degree bend limit for ventilating pipes; that is a raceway rule elsewhere. Not B: 502.128(1) requires the pipes to lead to a source of clean air outside of buildings, not into attic space. Not D: 502.128(2) requires the outer ends to be screened against small animals or birds, not fitted with hinged openings.
open-book-exam-#9-013.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: motor. Start with 502.128, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.

open-book-exam-#9-015.prompt: Boxes that enclose devices or utilization equipment that projects more than ___ rearward from the mounting plane of the box shall have a depth that is not less than the depth of the equipment plus 1/4 inch.

Boxes that enclose devices or utilization equipment that projects more than 48 mm (17/8 in.) rearward from the mounting plane of the box shall have a depth that is not less than the depth of the equipment plus 6 mm (1/4 in.).

Correct: D — 1 7/8". 314.24(B)(1) applies to equipment projecting more than 48 mm (1 7/8 inches) rearward from the mounting plane. Not A: 1/4 inch is the extra depth added to the equipment depth, not the projection that triggers the rule. Not B: 1/2 inch is the rear clearance for center-entry wiring in 314.24(B)(4), not the large-equipment trigger. Not C: 3/4 inch is not a threshold in 314.24(B); the large-equipment rule starts above 1 7/8 inches.

open-book-exam-#9-016.gist: A separately installed lug or splice has its own temperature rating, and that rating limits the conductor ampacity at that point. The question asks whose temperature rating sets the limit.

open-book-exam-#9-018.gist: Upsizing wire for voltage drop does not turn a 20-ampere circuit into a bigger one. The question asks what the overcurrent device still decides when larger conductors are used.

open-book-exam-#9-025.reference_text:
Article 100 Definitions — Luminaire
Luminaire. A complete lighting unit consisting of a light source such as a lamp or lamps, together with the parts designed to position the light source and connect it to the power supply. It may also include parts to protect the light source or the ballast or to distribute the light. A lampholder itself is not a luminaire. (CMP—18)
